dithercnDithered globe hero

A Bayer dither engine plus examples, installed via the shadcn registry

dithercn draws every surface as ordered-dither cells tied to your shadcn theme tokens, so a globe, an aurora shader and a headline fill all share one pixel grid and palette. The components install as plain source into your project, so you edit them like your own code instead of configuring a black-box package.

npx shadcn@latest add https://dithercn.dev/r/dither-globe.json
<Aurora className="absolute inset-x-0 top-0 -z-20 h-[62%]"
  color="green" tipColor="purple" curtains={4} direction="down" mask="bottom" />
<DitherGlobe
  markers={[SF, NYC, LDN, FRA, SGP, TYO, SYD, GRU].map((at) => ({ at }))}
  arcs={[{ from: SF, to: LDN }, { from: NYC, to: FRA, color: "green" }]}
  start={-30} tilt={28} speed={5} cell={3} matrix="bayer4" />
<DitherText as="h1" fill="gradient" direction="down" to={0.45}>
  Ship to every edge at once.
</DitherText>

dithercnDithered ops dashboard

A Bayer dither engine plus examples, installed via the shadcn registry

The chart and interface examples render as plain SVG built from whole dither cells, snapped to device pixels, so bars, gauges and heatmap squares step through crisp Bayer densities rather than opacity. Paper ShadersLive dithering shader

Zero-dependency WebGL shaders for React or vanilla JS

Paper's Dithering shader runs 2-colour ordered or random dithering over seven animated sources (sphere, warp, swirl, ripple...) entirely on the GPU in one small fragment shader. Every parameter is a prop, so matrix size, pixel size and ink colour can change live without remounting the canvas.

npm i @paper-design/shaders-react
<Dithering
  colorBack={c.back}
  colorFront={c.front}
  shape={shape}      // "sphere" | "warp" | "simplex" | "swirl" | ...
  type={type}        // "random" | "2x2" | "4x4" | "8x8"
  size={size}
  speed={1}
  offsetX={off.x + baseX}
  offsetY={off.y + baseY}
/>

three.js AsciiEffectLive 3D as ASCII

three.js add-on that renders any WebGL scene as text

AsciiEffect samples the WebGL frame each tick and rewrites it as a grid of real DOM characters, so the output is selectable text you can tint, glow and style with CSS. Swapping the character ramp changes the look completely, from classic terminal to Unicode shade blocks.

npm i three
import { AsciiEffect } from "three/examples/jsm/effects/AsciiEffect.js";

const CHARSETS = { classic: " .:-=+*#%@", blocks: " ░▒▓█", binary: " 01" };
effect = new AsciiEffect(renderer, CHARSETS[charsetName], { invert: true, resolution: res });
stage.prepend(effect.domElement);
effect.setSize(w, h);
// every frame
effect.render(scene, camera);

pixi-filtersCRT filter rack

Community WebGL filter collection for PixiJS v8

pixi-filters bundles dozens of stackable post-process shaders (CRT, RGB split, glitch, pixelate, ASCII, old film, bloom) that attach to any PixiJS container as a plain filters array. Order in the array is the order of the effect chain, so you can build a CRT pipeline in a few lines.

npm i pixi.js pixi-filters
const crt = new CRTFilter({ curvature: 4, lineWidth: 2.2, lineContrast: 0.35, noise: 0.12, noiseSize: 1.2, vignetting: 0.32 });
const rgb = new RGBSplitFilter({ red: [-3, 0], green: [0, 1], blue: [3, 0] });
const glitch = new GlitchFilter({ slices: 12, offset: 40, fillMode: 2, average: false });
const ascii = new AsciiFilter({ size: 9, color: "#7dffcf", replaceColor: false });
// order matters: pixel/ascii first (they quantise), CRT last (it curves the result)
const ORDER = ["pixel", "ascii", "film", "bloom", "glitch", "rgb", "crt"];
const on = ORDER.map((id) => RACK.find((r) => r.id === id)).filter((r) => r.on).map((r) => r.f);
app.stage.filters = on.length ? on : null;

postprocessingPixel, ASCII & halftone diorama

pmndrs post-processing effect library for three.js

postprocessing merges multiple effects into a single fullscreen shader pass, which keeps a stack of bloom, vignette and stylising effects cheap. Its PixelationEffect, ASCIIEffect and DotScreenEffect turn any three.js scene into pixel art, glyphs or print halftone with one constructor.

npm i three postprocessing
composer.addPass(new RenderPass(scene, camera));
composer.addPass(new EffectPass(camera, bloom, vignette));
const asciiTexture = new ASCIITexture({ characters: " .:-+*=%@#", font: "Space Mono", fontSize: 54, size: 1024, cellCount: 16 });
const MODES = {
  pixel: { make: (v) => new PixelationEffect(v), set: (e, v) => (e.granularity = v) },
  ascii: { make: (v) => new ASCIIEffect({ asciiTexture, cellSize: v, color: null }), set: (e, v) => (e.cellSize = v) },
  halftone: { make: (v) => new DotScreenEffect({ angle: Math.PI * 0.25, scale: v }), set: (e, v) => (e.scale = v) },
};
effect = MODES[mode].make(amount);
composer.addPass(new EffectPass(camera, effect));

Ratzillaratatui dashboard in WASM

Ratatui terminal UIs compiled to WebAssembly for the browser

Ratzilla runs Rust's ratatui widget library in a web page: the same Gauge, Sparkline, BarChart, Table and braille Canvas you'd use in a real terminal, drawn by a WebGL2 glyph-atlas backend. The layout is ratatui's constraint solver, so the dashboard restacks into one column on a phone. Everything here, including the braille world map and lissajous, is Rust compiled to a single .wasm.

cargo add ratzilla
let options = WebGl2BackendOptions::new()
    .grid_id("term")
    .font_atlas_config(FontAtlasConfig::dynamic(
        &["JetBrains Mono", "DejaVu Sans Mono", "Noto Sans Mono"],
        pick_font_size(),
    ));
let backend = WebGl2Backend::new_with_options(options).map_err(js_err)?;
let mut terminal = Terminal::new(backend).map_err(js_err)?;
terminal.draw_web(move |f| { /* ratatui widgets */ });
// WORLD tab: braille Canvas
ctx.draw(&Map { color: MAPGREY, resolution: MapResolution::High });

dotmaxBraille effects in WASM

Rust crate for high-density braille terminal graphics

dotmax packs 2×4 dots into every Unicode braille cell, so a terminal (or a <pre>) gets eight times the pixels of plain text. This is the crate's real BrailleGrid and line/circle/colour primitives compiled to wasm32, with the terminal-only modules stripped, writing coloured braille text into a <pre> that re-fits on resize. Five effects: plasma, black hole, ribbons and more.

cargo add dotmax
// Event horizon: rasterise a filled disc with dotmax, then AND it out.
let mut hole = BrailleGrid::new(self.cols, self.rows).expect("grid");
let _ = draw_circle_filled(&mut hole, ci, cj, horizon as u32);
let mut pat = self.grid.get_raw_patterns().to_vec();
for (p, m) in pat.iter_mut().zip(hole.get_raw_patterns()) {
    *p &= !m;
}
self.grid.set_raw_patterns(&pat);
let _ = draw_line_colored(&mut self.grid, lx, ly, x, y, c, None);

HTML5 Canvas 2D API that draws in Unicode braille dots

back.stroke(); front.stroke(); verts.stroke();

rot.jsTorchlit braille dungeon

Roguelike toolkit: glyph display, map generators, FOV, pathfinding, lighting

rot.js gives you the whole roguelike stack in the browser: a character-cell Display, dungeon generators, shadowcasting field of view, A* paths and coloured light. Here a Digger dungeon is generated to the viewport, walls are drawn as braille masonry, and a flickering torch plus ROT.Lighting glow decide what you see. Leave it idle and an A* auto-explorer loots, fights and descends.

npm i rot-js
const digger = new ROT.Map.Digger(W, H, {
  roomWidth: [4, 11], roomHeight: [3, 7], corridorLength: [2, 7], dugPercentage: 0.4,
});
digger.create((x, y, v) => { if (!v) tiles[idx(x, y)] = FLOOR; });
fov = new ROT.FOV.PreciseShadowcasting(transparent, { topology: 8 });
lighting = new ROT.Lighting((x, y) => (transparent(x, y) ? 0.22 : 0), { range: 7, passes: 2 });
lighting.setFOV(fov);

textmode.jsLive glyph sketches

Real-time ASCII and textmode creative coding on a WebGL2 grid

textmode.js has a p5-style sketch API (push, rotate, rect, torus, lights), but it rasterises everything into a grid of characters on the GPU. The torus uses the library's own pointLight and torus(), so the lighting is computed per cell. Four sketches (tunnel, lit solids, flow field, copper bars) run on its bundled CP437 pixel font.

npm i textmode.js
t.push();
t.ambientLight(lo[0] * 0.6, lo[1] * 0.6, lo[2] * 0.6);
t.pointLight(hi[0], hi[1], hi[2], ptr.x * 1.6, ptr.y * 1.6, m * 0.9);
t.rotateX(time * 38 + ptr.dragY * 6);
t.rotateY(time * 52 + ptr.dragX * 6);
t.char('○');
t.charColor(255, 255, 255);
t.torus(m * 0.3, m * 0.11);
t.pop();

play.coreASCII program runner

Andreas Gysin's runtime for ASCII programs written as per-cell functions

play.core is the engine behind the ASCII Playground: a program exports a main(coord, context, cursor) function that returns one character per cell, and the runner sizes the grid from font metrics and renders it as DOM text. Four programs run here: SDF braille metaballs, copper bars, braille rain and an adapted Doom flame. It is unpublished on npm and vendored from GitHub.

git clone https://github.com/ertdfgcvb/play.core
function field(x, y) {
  let d = 1e9
  for (const b of balls) {
    p.x = x - b.x; p.y = y - b.y
    d = opSmoothUnion(d, sdCircle(p, b.r), k)
  }
  return d
}
run(wrap(prog, ctl, onFirstFrame), {
  element: el, renderer: 'text',
  fontFamily: "'Iosevka', monospace", color: '#ffb000',
})

ascii-magic-artAnimated ASCII gallery

634 animated ASCII art pieces with a player and glyph looks

Each piece is a tiny ES module whose draw(t) returns a frame of text plus a colour layer.   if (state.stop) state.stop();

  state.stop = play(art, state.mod, {
    look: { look: state.look }, t0,
    onFrame: (_f, t) => { state.t = t; },

cli-spinnersLive spinner gallery

Sindre Sorhus's JSON collection of 90 terminal loading spinners

cli-spinners is just data: each spinner is a list of frames and an interval, which is why it works in any terminal library or web page. All 71 non-emoji spinners run at their native interval from one rAF loop, colour-coded by family (braille dots, lines, blocks, arrows). The selected one drives a fake install line with a braille progress bar.

npm i cli-spinners
import cliSpinners from 'cli-spinners';
for (const name of allNames) {
  const { interval, frames } = cliSpinners[name];
  if (frames.some(f => EMOJI.test(f))) continue;
}
// one rAF loop, per-spinner elapsed time
for (const s of spinners) {
  if (!s.vis) continue;
  const i = Math.floor(clock / s.interval) % s.frames.length;
  if (i !== s.idx) { s.idx = i; s.glyph.textContent = s.frames[i]; }
}

ascii-magic-artASCII empty states

Library empty-state and loader pieces used as real app UI

ascii-magic-art ships whole categories of empty-state and loader pieces. A mail-client mock uses them as illustrations, cropped to the drawing so real HTML supplies the heading and buttons. Each tab cycles empty → loading (skeleton, progress and upload loaders) → results, and the Online toggle switches to an offline-plug animation.

npm i ascii-magic-art
function crop(mod, { top = 0, rows, left = 0, cols }) {
  const m = mod.meta;
  return {
    meta: { ...m, rows, cols },
    default() {
      const draw = mod.default();
      return (t) => { const f = draw(t); return typeof f === 'string' ? cut(f) : { ...f, text: cut(f.text), color: cut(f.color) }; };
    },
  };
}
S.stop = play(art, S.mod, { look: { look: 'original' }, t0, onFrame: (_f, t) => { S.t = t; } });

Matrix digital rain (Rezmason)Seven-version code rain

Film-accurate Matrix code rain on WebGL, configured by URL params

Each glyph is an MSDF texture sampled in a fragment shader, so the film fonts stay sharp at any size, and the rain is simulated on the GPU in ping-pong framebuffers before a bloom pyramid and palette pass. One config object switches between the 1999 grid, the Resurrections glyph set, volumetric 3D rain, polar Coptic ripples and a slanted gothic storm with thunder.

git clone https://github.com/Rezmason/matrix
import makeConfig from '../../vendor/matrix/js/config.js';
import startRain from '../../vendor/matrix/js/regl/main.js';

const config = bundleURLs(
  makeConfig({ version: v.id, renderer: 'regl', suppressWarnings: 'true' }),
);
config.resolution = resolutionFor();

const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
stage.appendChild(canvas);
await startRain(canvas, config); // resolves once shaders + MSDF textures are ready and frames run

BBS-era ANSI/XBIN/ADF art rendered to canvas with real CP437 fonts

glyphcssASCII mesh foundry

3D polygon meshes rasterized as text in one <pre>

glyphcss projects real 3D geometry (OBJ, glTF, STL, .vox or its own primitives) and rasterizes it into a single monospace <pre>, with no WebGL, no canvas and no per-polygon DOM nodes. The same scene switches between Lambert-shaded ramps, 2×2 quadrant blocks, hidden-line braille wireframe and contour-tracing ink mode, so the output is selectable text you can style with CSS.

npm i glyphcss
const camera = createGlyphPerspectiveCamera({ rotX: 62, rotY: 30, zoom: 1 });
const scene = createGlyphScene(host, {
  mode: 'solid', charMode: 'ascii', glyphPalette: 'detail',
  autoSize: true, camera, smoothShading: true,
  directionalLight: { direction: [0.45, -0.55, 0.7], color: '#fff1dc', intensity: 0.95 },
  ambientLight: { color: '#b4bcff', intensity: 0.72 },
});
createGlyphOrbitControls(scene, { wheel: false, pan: false, animate: { speed: 0.35, axis: 'y' } });
scene.add(parametricSurfacePolygons({ x: X, y: Y, z: Z, wrapRows: true, wrapCols: true },
  { color: (ri) => ramp(KNOT, ri / rows) }));
scene.setOptions({ mode: 'wireframe', charMode: 'braille', hiddenLines: 'hide' });

ASCII FXShape vs brightness ASCII

Shape-aware ASCII rendering for React, WebGPU with exact CPU fallback

Most ASCII filters pick a glyph by how much ink it has; ASCII FX matches each cell's 8×8 sample block against every glyph's real rasterised mask, so diagonals become / and \ and type stays legible. The split view runs the library's own brightness-ramp matcher against its structural matcher on the same font and grid, in WebGPU compute or bit-identical CPU workers.

npm i @ascii-fx/react @ascii-fx/core
const profile = await createAsciiProfile({ fontFamily: 'JetBrains Mono', charset: 'ascii' });

<AsciiCanvas ref={asciiRef} source={source} renderMode="manual"
  profile={profile} columns={grid.columns} rows={grid.rows}
  color={color} background={BG} fit="contain" />

// per frame: paint the source canvas, re-match it
drawScene(ctx, source.width, source.height, t);
asciiRef.current?.render();

/>

PretextWalden flows around the moon

DOM-free multiline text measurement and layout in pure TypeScript

Pretext measures and line-breaks text without touching the DOM, so you can re-layout a paragraph against arbitrary shapes every frame. Here two justified columns of Walden are re-broken around a draggable moon (and its own label) on each animation frame, using a per-row width and a shared cursor across columns, in well under 2 ms.

npm i @chenglou/pretext
prepared = prepareWithSegments(WALDEN, `400 ${fs}px "Fraunces Variable"`); // once per font

// every frame: each row gets its own corridor(s) around the moon
for (const [a, b] of spans) {
  const avail = b - a;
  let range = layoutNextLineRange(prepared, avail, cursor);
  if (!range) { cursor = undefined; range = layoutNextLineRange(prepared, avail, cursor); }
  const line = materializeLineRange(prepared, range);
  drawLine(line.text, a, y + fs * 1.05, avail, range.width > avail * 0.72, near);
  cursor = range.end;
}

Splitting.jsVariable-font CSS wave

Splits text into spans with CSS custom-property indexes

Splitting.js makes one pass over the DOM, wrapping each word and character and giving it --char-index and --char-total custom properties; everything after that is plain CSS. A registered @property sweeps a highlight across the word, and each letter computes its own variable-font weight, softness, colour and lift from its distance to it.

npm i splitting
Splitting({ target: '[data-splitting]', by: 'chars' });

/* CSS does the rest */
@property --hi { syntax: '<number>'; inherits: true; initial-value: 0; }
.wave .char {
  --d: max(var(--char-index) - var(--hi), var(--hi) - var(--char-index));
  font-variation-settings:
    'wght' clamp(120, 900 - var(--d) * 200, 900),
    'SOFT' clamp(0, 100 - var(--d) * 40, 100);
}

three-slugDiving into a curve

Eric Lengyel's Slug glyph algorithm, ported to three.js

three-slug evaluates each glyph's quadratic Béziers in the fragment shader, so text has exact coverage at any zoom, and it splices into MeshStandardMaterial for real lighting and shadows. The camera dives from a lit word into one curve, shown with its control polygon, down to about ×2,000 where the edge is still a one-pixel ramp; the bitmap dot-grid wall goes soft at that zoom.

npm i three-slug three
const data = await new SlugGenerator().generateFromBuffer(buf.slice(0));

const geometry = new SlugGeometry(256);
const material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color, roughness: 0.38, metalness: 0.05, side: THREE.DoubleSide });
const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
injectSlug(mesh, material, data);
geometry.addText(str, data, { fontScale: fs, startX: x, startY: y, justify: 'left' });
mesh.castShadow = true;
scene.add(mesh);

pr.lines.forEach((line, i) => {
  const slot = pr.slots[i]; // column position: right offset + top
  const pitch = line.fontSize * LS;
  col.style.cssText = `right:${slot.xPos}px;top:${slot.yStart}px;width:${pitch}px;height:${slot.height}px;font-size:${line.fontSize}px;line-height:${pitch}px`;

});

Wavefont + LinefontText-only oscilloscope

Variable fonts that draw bar and line charts from characters

Each character U+0100–U+017F is one data value: Wavefont draws it as a bar, Linefont as a connected line segment. So waveforms, spectra and sparklines are ordinary selectable text, styled by variable axes for width, roundness and alignment. Every trace here is a string rewritten 30 times a second; the raw toggle shows the actual characters.

npm i wavefont linefont
import wf from 'wavefont';
import lf from 'linefont';
// linefont: signed trace mapped to 0..127, centred at 64
trace.textContent = lf(Array.from(tr, (v) => 64 + v * 58));
// wavefont (YELA 0 = centred bars): magnitude envelope
env.textContent = wf(Array.from(en, (v) => Math.abs(v) * 118 + 4));
/* css */
.bars { font-family: wavefont;
  font-variation-settings: 'wght' 520, 'ROND' 70, 'YELA' -100; }

function remount(sp) {
  const fresh = sp.cloneNode(true);
  fresh.classList.remove('open');
  configure(fresh); // setAttribute('density' | 'scale' | 'max-velocity' | ...)
  sp.replaceWith(fresh);
  wire(fresh);
}

TorphAnagram engine

Dependency-free text morphing for React, Vue, Svelte and vanilla JS

Torph diffs the old and new string and slides shared letters to their new positions, so 'listen' becomes 'silent' with every letter travelling and nothing fading out. n1.update('$' + rev.toLocaleString('en', { minimumFractionDigits: 2 }));

// editable field: caret matching instead of place matching
input.addEventListener('input', () => live.update(input.value, input.selectionStart));

harfbuzzjsShaping x-ray

The HarfBuzz text-shaping engine compiled to WebAssembly

harfbuzzjs exposes what the browser does internally: which glyph IDs a string becomes, their advances and offsets, and which code points each glyph came from. Here Arabic letters change their joining form as each new letter is typed, Devanagari moves its i-matra in front of the consonant and lifts the reph above it, and EB Garamond builds ligatures and fractions. Glyph outlines are drawn straight from glyphToPath, and you can toggle each OpenType feature to see the result change.

npm i harfbuzzjs
const font = new hb.Font(new hb.Face(new hb.Blob(await res.arrayBuffer())));

const buffer = new hb.Buffer();
buffer.addText('مرحبا بكم');
buffer.guessSegmentProperties();
hb.shape(font, buffer, [new hb.Feature('init', 0)]); // switch a feature off

for (const g of buffer.getGlyphInfosAndPositions()) {
  path.setAttribute('d', font.glyphToPath(g.codepoint)); // glyph id → SVG outline
  pen += g.xAdvance;                                     // g.cluster → source code point
}

A typewriter effect for React with pacing, pauses and per-character hooks

Windups types out any React children one character at a time and handles timing for you: it pauses on punctuation by default, and <Pace> and <Pause> set a speed or a beat inside a line. <CharWrapper> wraps each character in its own element, which is how the wobbly and trembling words animate. <OnChar> drives the frog's mouth and the optional synth blips. <Linebreaker> works out line breaks before typing starts, so words never jump to the next line halfway through.

      <Pause ms={200} /> and some <CharWrapper element={Shaky}>TREMBLE IN FEAR</CharWrapper>!
      Let me <Pace ms={16}>ramble-on-at-tremendous-speed</Pace>.
    </OnChar>
  </WindupChildren>
</Linebreaker>

magnetTypeVariable-font cursor field

Per-word variable-font axes driven by cursor proximity

magnetType wraps each word in a span and sets its font-variation-settings from the pointer's distance, so a paragraph swells heavier and wider around the cursor and relaxes behind it. Here a Fraunces headline (wght/opsz/SOFT) and a Roboto Flex column (wght/wdth/GRAD) each run their own field, with a phantom cursor drifting on a Lissajous path when idle.

  radius: 200,
  falloff: 'linear',
  scope: 'document',
  props: { opacity: [0.45, 1] },
});

FloodTextPer-character axis tide

Variable-font waves washing through text, one character at a time

FloodText wraps every grapheme and drives weight, width, oblique angle or opacity along a travelling sine, so each letter sits at its own point on the wave. Line breaks stay locked and kerning is preserved while glyph widths change, so the poem never reflows. This demo layers axes on a Roboto Flex poem, with controls for direction and swell and a WCAG pause button.

const chars = applyFloodText(poem, original);
const stop = startFloodText(chars, {
  effect: ['wght', 'wdth', 'oblique', 'opacity'],
  amplitudes: { wght: 247, wdth: 30, oblique: 6.5, opacity: 0.23 },
  period: 4.5, density: 1.6, direction: 'diagonal-down',
});

CobeGlobe with anchored labels

A 5 kB WebGL dotted globe with markers and arcs

Cobe draws a Fibonacci-sampled dot-matrix Earth in a single fragment shader, with no three.js and zero deps. Version 2 adds arcs and exposes every marker as a CSS anchor, so the labels here are plain DOM elements placed with CSS anchor positioning and faded by a --cobe-visible-* variable.

npm i cobe
const globe = createGlobe(canvas, {
  width: 600, height: 600, phi, theta, dark: 1,
  mapSamples: 20000, baseColor: [0.22, 0.24, 0.32],
  markerColor: [1, 0.52, 0.26], arcColor: [1, 0.62, 0.38],
  markers: cities.map((c) => ({ location: c.loc, size: 0.035, id: c.id })),
  arcs: arcs.map(([a, b]) => ({ from: byId[a].loc, to: byId[b].loc })),
});
// labels: plain DOM, positioned by CSS anchor positioning
el.style.positionAnchor = `--cobe-${c.id}`;
el.style.opacity = `var(--cobe-visible-${c.id}, 0)`;
function frame() { globe.update({ phi, theta }); requestAnimationFrame(frame); }

OGLFlowmap poster distortion

Minimal WebGL library with a three.js-like API

OGL is a small, dependency-free WebGL abstraction with renderer, program, mesh and an extras folder. Its Flowmap helper ping-pongs render targets to record cursor velocity, and here that velocity drives a per-channel RGB-split warp of a procedurally drawn poster.

npm i ogl
const flowmap = new Flowmap(gl, { falloff: 0.28, dissipation: 0.965 });
const program = new Program(gl, { vertex, fragment,
  uniforms: { tWater: { value: texture }, tFlow: flowmap.uniform, res: { value: [0, 0, 1, 1] } } });
const mesh = new Mesh(gl, { geometry: new Triangle(gl), program });

function update() {
  flowmap.mouse.copy(mouse);
  flowmap.velocity.lerp(velocity, velocity.len() ? 0.5 : 0.1);
  flowmap.update();
  renderer.render({ scene: mesh });
}

TypeGPUGPU boids murmuration

Type-safe WebGPU toolkit: typed buffers, layouts and shaders in TypeScript

TypeGPU describes GPU memory with schemas (d.struct, d.arrayOf, d.atomic) so buffer writes, bind-group layouts and the generated WGSL bindings all come from one typed definition. Here thousands of boids run in a three-pass spatial-grid compute pipeline and draw as flapping chevrons into a fading float accumulation buffer.

npm i typegpu
const Boid = d.struct({ pos: d.vec2f, vel: d.vec2f }).$name('Boid');
const simLayout = tgpu.bindGroupLayout({
  params: { uniform: Params },
  src: { storage: (n) => d.arrayOf(Boid, n), access: 'readonly' },
  dst: { storage: (n) => d.arrayOf(Boid, n), access: 'mutable' },
  counts: { storage: (n) => d.arrayOf(d.atomic(d.u32), n), access: 'mutable' },
  items: { storage: (n) => d.arrayOf(d.u32, n), access: 'mutable' },
}).$idx(0);
const boidsA = root.createBuffer(d.arrayOf(Boid, MAX_BOIDS), seed).$usage('storage');
// typed layout -> WGSL struct + @group/@binding declarations
device.createShaderModule({ code: tgpu.resolve({ template, externals: { L } }) });

color4bg ships 14 ready-made background generators (wavy satin, contour swirls, low-poly mosaics, floating cubes) built on a tiny OGL core. Each one takes up to six colours and a seed, so the same pattern reproduces exactly and a palette swap is one colors() call, no image files involved.

npm i color4bg
import { WavyWavesBg } from 'color4bg'

const bg = new WavyWavesBg({
  dom: 'hero',
  colors: ['#2b1055', '#7597de', '#d5458f', '#f7b267', '#1b1b3a', '#6c3fb5'],
  seed: 1000,
  loop: true,
})
// live palette swap, no rebuild
bg.colors(['#03203c', '#0e7490', '#22d3ee', '#1e40af', '#020617', '#5eead4'])

ShadersLayered liquid hero

200+ WebGPU shader effects as composable framework components

Every effect is a component: generators like MeshGradient, Aurora and Satin stack like Figma layers with real blend modes, and filters (CursorRipples, Dither, FilmGrain) apply to everything above them. Props accept pointer drivers such as { type: 'mouse-position' }, so cursor-reactive motion takes no animation code. This hero switches between four compositions of one <Shader>.

npm i shaders
<Shader className="shader" disableTelemetry onUnavailable={onUnavailable}>
  <LinearGradient colorA="#010208" colorB="#0a1a40" start={{ x: 0.5, y: 1 }} end={{ x: 0.5, y: 0 }} />
  <Aurora colorA="#8a2cff" colorB="#2bffb2" colorC="#1a8cff" intensity={95} curtainCount={5}
    speed={4} waviness={65} rayDensity={26} height={155} blendMode="screen"
    center={{ type: 'mouse-position', y: 0, smoothing: 0.85, reach: 0.35 }} />
  <Glow threshold={0.35} size={42} intensity={0.9} />
  <CursorRipples intensity={12} radius={0.6} decay={6} chromaticSplit={2} />
  <FilmGrain strength={0.16} />
</Shader>

ShadersGlass lens playground

200+ WebGPU shader effects as composable framework components

The vanilla shaders/js API takes a JSON component tree, so an image filter is just ImageTexture plus an effect: a refracting Glass solid (sphere, torus, gem, blob) with chromatic aberration and frost, FlutedGlass, CMYK Halftone or a CRTScreen. Sliders call shader.update() live, and mode switches cross-fade between trees that share one WebGPU device.

npm i shaders
const { createShader, createSharedDevice } = await import('shaders/js')
const gpu = await createSharedDevice()
const live = await createShader(canvas, { components: [
  { type: 'ImageTexture', id: 'img', props: { url: srcUrl, objectFit: 'cover' } },
  { type: 'Glass', id: 'fx', props: {
    center: { type: 'mouse-position', smoothing: 0.55, momentum: 0.25 },
    shape: JSON.stringify({ type: 'torus3D', radius: 0.25, tube: 0.1, rotX: 62 }),
    refraction: 0.9, aberration: 0.9, blur: 0, scale: 1.05 } },
] }, { gpu, disableTelemetry: true })
input.oninput = () => live.update('fx', { refraction: +input.value })

Shader Lab (basement.studio)Dither, CRT, ASCII, halftone stacks

basement.studio's runtime for layered Shader Lab compositions

npm i @basementstudio/shader-lab three
layer('dither', 'effect', 'dithering', {
  algorithm: 'bayer-8x8', colorMode: 'duo-tone', levels: 3,

  shadowColor: '#0b0b0c', highlightColor: '#ff4d00',
}),
source = new ShaderLabCanvasSource(configFor(current), {
  canvas, width: view.w, height: view.h, pixelRatio: view.dpr,
})
await source.initialize()
// every frame: pointer-driven params are just data
source.setConfig(configFor(current))
source.update(clock, dt)

use-shader-fxFluid-stirred marble

FunTech's hook kit of ready-made shader FX for react-three-fiber

Each hook (useFluid, useNoise, useBuffer, useBlank) renders into its own FBO and returns a texture, so effects chain like nodes: here a Navier-Stokes fluid's flow map is fed into useNoise's built-in mixSrc UV-displacement to stir a domain-warped marble field. v2's shared 'basicFx' layer gives every hook mix, levels, HSV and duotone options without writing GLSL.

npm i @funtech-inc/use-shader-fx
const fluid = useFluid({ size, dpr: 0.32, pressureIterations: 16, forceBias: 28 })
const noise = useNoise({
  size, dpr: NOISE_DPR, fbmOctaves: 3,
  mixSrc: { src: flow.texture, uv: { factor: 0.55, mixMap: { src: flow.texture } } },
})
const blank = useBlank({ size, dpr, uniforms, vertexShader, fragmentShader })
useFrame((state) => {
  fluid.render({ ...state, pointer: ptr.current }, { radius })
  flow.render(state)
  noise.render(state, { warpStrength: n.warp, timeStrength: n.speed })
  blank.render(state)
})

three-good-godraysPerforated geodesic lantern

Raymarched volumetric god rays for three.js, occluded by real shadow maps

A postprocessing pass that raymarches each pixel's view ray through the light's shadow map, so shafts are cut by the actual geometry rather than smeared radially in screen space. Here a point light sits inside an 80-panel perforated icosphere: every hole throws its own beam, and the dark wedges between them rotate with the lattice. Density, attenuation, color and step count are live parameters.

npm i three-good-godrays postprocessing three
renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true
const light = new THREE.PointLight(0xffb46e, 140, 0, 1.4)
light.castShadow = true
const composer = new EffectComposer(renderer, { frameBufferType: THREE.HalfFloatType })
composer.addPass(new RenderPass(scene, camera))
const godrays = new GodraysPass(light, camera, {
  density: 1 / 60, maxDensity: 0.62, distanceAttenuation: 2.2,
  color: new THREE.Color(0xffa255),
  raymarchSteps: 60, resolutionScale: 0.5,
  blur: { variance: 0.12, kernelSize: KernelSize.MEDIUM },
})
composer.addPass(godrays)

World Labs' gaussian splat renderer for three.js

Spark draws photo-captured 3D gaussian splats next to ordinary three.js meshes and treats every splat as editable on the GPU. Here a 240k-splat CC0 cactus scan is relit with SplatEdit SDF light spheres and scattered by a custom dyno shader-graph block. It reads .spz, .ply, .splat, .ksplat and .sog files.

glow.add(new SplatEditSdf({ type: SplatEditSdfType.SPHERE, radius: 0.25, color }));

three.js WebGPU + TSLProcedural node-material blob

three.js shading language: node materials written in JavaScript

TSL builds shaders from composable JavaScript nodes (noise, palettes, fresnel, uniforms) and compiles them to WGSL for WebGPU or GLSL for the WebGL2 fallback. Displacement, contour bands and rim glow here are all node graphs on a MeshPhysicalNodeMaterial, with no shader strings. The badge shows which backend your browser got.

npm i three
import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu';
import { Fn, time, vec3, positionLocal, normalLocal, mx_fractal_noise_float, cos } from 'three/tsl';

const field = Fn(([p]) => mx_fractal_noise_float(p.mul(1.35).add(vec3(0, time.mul(0.18), 0)), 4, 2.0, 0.5, 1.0));
const palette = Fn(([t]) => uA.add(uB.mul(cos(uC.mul(t).add(uD).mul(6.28318)))));

const material = new THREE.MeshPhysicalNodeMaterial({ clearcoat: 1 });
const n = field(positionLocal);
material.positionNode = positionLocal.add(normalLocal.mul(n.mul(0.28)));
material.colorNode = palette(n.mul(5.0).add(time.mul(0.12)));
const renderer = new THREE.WebGPURenderer({ antialias: true }); // WebGL2 fallback built in

Theatre.jsKeyframed cinematic camera

Motion-design keyframe sequencer for the web and three.js

Theatre.js plays back keyframed, bezier-eased sequences of any props: camera position, look-at target, FOV and light color here. The project state is the same JSON its visual Studio exports, so @theatre/core alone (Apache-2.0, no editor UI) drives the animation. The custom timeline scrubs sheet.sequence.position directly.

npm i @theatre/core
const project = getProject('Monolith', { state: buildState() });
const sheet = project.sheet('Scene');
const cam = sheet.object('Camera', {
  position: types.compound({ x: types.number(0), y: types.number(1.4), z: types.number(15) }),
  fov: types.number(30, { range: [10, 90] }),
});
cam.onValuesChange(({ position, fov }) => {
  camera.position.set(position.x, position.y, position.z);
  camera.fov = fov; camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
});
project.ready.then(() => sheet.sequence.play({ iterationCount: Infinity }));

CustomShaderMaterialOne shader, four materials

Extend three.js built-in materials with your own shader code

three-custom-shader-material injects your vertex/fragment code into any built-in material and keeps its lighting, shadows and PBR features. The same displacement-plus-recomputed-normals shader runs here on Physical (iridescent clearcoat), Toon, Matcap and Normal base materials. You write csm_Position and csm_Normal instead of rewriting a lighting model.

npm i three-custom-shader-material three
const material = new CustomShaderMaterial({
  baseMaterial: THREE.MeshPhysicalMaterial, // or MeshToonMaterial, MeshMatcapMaterial…
  vertexShader: `
    void main() {
      vec3 p0 = position + normal * disp(position);
      csm_Position = p0;
      csm_Normal = normalize(cross(pt - p0, pb - p0));
    }`,
  uniforms,
  roughness: 0.18, clearcoat: 1, iridescence: 1,
});

gradient.waveAmplitude = from + (to - from) * e;

Takram three-geospatialGolden hour over the Alps

Physically based sky, aerial perspective and volumetric clouds for three.js

Implements Bruneton's precomputed atmospheric scattering in real ECEF coordinates: you give it a lat/long and a Date, and it computes the true sun position, sky radiance, sunlight transmittance and haze over distance. Here the procedural ridges fade into warm haze as you scrub through a real Alpine sunset. On hardware GPUs the companion @takram/three-clouds package adds ray-marched cloud layers lit by the same atmosphere.

npm i @takram/three-atmosphere @takram/three-clouds @takram/three-geospatial postprocessing three
const aerial = new AerialPerspectiveEffect(camera, { sky: true, sun: true, moon: true })
aerial.worldToECEFMatrix.copy(worldToECEF) // local ENU frame at 46.56N 7.98E
Object.assign(aerial, textures)            // precomputed Bruneton LUTs
sunLight.transmittanceTexture = textures.transmittanceTexture
skyLight.irradianceTexture = textures.irradianceTexture
composer.addPass(new EffectPass(camera, clouds, aerial, bloom, toneMap))

getSunDirectionECEF(date, sunECEF)
aerial.sunDirection.copy(sunECEF)
sunLight.sunDirection.copy(sunECEF); sunLight.update()
skyLight.sunDirection.copy(sunECEF); skyLight.update()

TSL TexturesProcedural swatch wall

Fifty-plus procedural three.js textures written in TSL node code

Pavel Boytchev's library turns each texture (planet, marble, tiger fur, fordite, Dyson sphere...) into a single TSL function that returns a color node, so it compiles to WGSL or GLSL and runs on WebGPU or the WebGL2 fallback with no image files. Every parameter, including the seed, can be a uniform: here twelve swatches drift by animating their seed, and a tap reseeds one.

npm i tsl-textures three
import { planet, marble, fordite } from 'tsl-textures';

const seed = uniform(i * 7.31 + 1.7);
const tex = s.fn({ ...s.p, seed });   // e.g. marble({ scale: 1.1, color, background, seed })
const mat = new THREE.MeshPhysicalNodeMaterial({ roughness: 0.42, clearcoat: 0.7 });
mat.colorNode = tex.mul(dim);
mat.roughnessNode = mix(float(0.62), float(0.22), luminance(tex).clamp(0, 1));

// animated param: the seed is a TSL uniform, drifting = flowing pattern
s.seed.value += ((s.seedBase + t * s.drift) - s.seed.value) * (1 - Math.exp(-dt * 3));

Shader ParkMorphing SDF sculpture

Write raymarched SDF shaders as plain JavaScript

You describe a 3D form with JS calls like sphere(), boxFrame(), noise() and mixGeo(), and Shader Park compiles them to a raymarched GLSL signed-distance field rendered on a three.js mesh. Shapes blend smoothly with no polygons, and uniforms like time, mouse and a click input drive them live.

npm i shader-park-core three
const spCode = `
  let click = input();
  let s = getSpace();
  let n = noise(s * 2.4 + vec3(0, 0, time * 0.35));
  metal(0.8);
  shine(0.9);
  rotateY(time * 0.25 + mouse.x * 2.2);
  boxFrame(vec3(0.5), 0.045 + abs(n) * 0.05);
  mixGeo(click);
  sphere(0.5 + n * 0.14);
`;
const mesh = createSculpture(spCode, () => ({ time: state.time, click: state.click, mouse: state.mouse }), { radius: 1.15, segments: 48 });

GL TransitionsGLSL transition slideshow

Open collection of 100+ GLSL image transitions

Every transition is one small GLSL function, transition(uv), that mixes two textures by a progress value, so the same file runs in a browser, a video editor or ffmpeg. The npm package ships the whole community collection with author and license metadata, and gl-transition renders any entry onto a WebGL canvas.

npm i gl-transitions gl-transition gl-texture2d
const usable = GLTransitions.filter((t) => !Object.values(t.paramsTypes).includes('sampler2D'));
const list = PICKS.map((n) => usable.find((t) => t.name === n)).filter(Boolean);

const getTransition = (t) => {
  if (!compiled.has(t.name)) compiled.set(t.name, createTransition(gl, t, { resizeMode: 'cover' }));
  return compiled.get(t.name);
};
textures = imgs.map((img) => createTexture(gl, img));

function drawFrame(p) {
  getTransition(list[tIndex]).draw(p, textures[from], textures[to], canvas.width, canvas.height);
}

blobsLayered morphing blobs

Seeded random blob shapes that morph smoothly

blobs generates organic closed shapes from a seed, point count and randomness value, then interpolates between any two of them, even with different point counts, without kinks.   animation.transition({ duration: layer.duration, timingFunction: 'ease', callback: loop, blobOptions: opts(layer, seeds[i]) });
};
animation.transition({ duration: 0, callback: loop, blobOptions: opts(layer, seeds[i]) });

// every frame, per layer
ctx.fill(animation.renderFrame());

VFX-JSGlitch gallery on real DOM

One call puts WebGL shaders on any img, video or text element

VFX-JS copies a live HTML element into a WebGL texture and redraws it each frame through a preset or custom GLSL shader, so headlines and images stay real, editable DOM. Uniforms can be functions, so pointer distance, scroll or app state feed the shader directly. Retype the headline here and the glitch follows your text.

npm i @vfx-js/core
vfx = VFX.init({ pixelRatio: Math.min(devicePixelRatio || 1, 2), scrollPadding: false });
// real <h1> + <em>: rasterised from the DOM, then shaded
vfx.add(hlWrap, { shader: glitchText, overflow: [12, 70, 12, 70], uniforms: uni(hlItem) });
vfx.add(acc, { shader: 'rainbow', overflow: 4 });
// <img> plates: custom GLSL fed by function uniforms (read every frame)
vfx.add(p.img, {
  shader: shaderFor[p.fx],
  uniforms: uni(it, { aspect, origin: () => it.origin }),
});
// retype the headline -> re-snapshot the DOM into the texture
await vfx.update(hlWrap);

glfx.jsSwirl lens photo tool

Evan Wallace's WebGL image-effects library with a chainable filter API

glfx.js runs classic photo filters (swirl, bulge/pinch, hex pixelate, CMYK halftone, ink, tilt-shift) as WebGL shaders and chains them into one draw call. Filters are positioned in pixel space, so you can attach a distortion lens to the pointer and change parameters on every frame. It dates from 2011 and still works under a modern bundler.

npm i glfx
const canvas = fx.canvas();
const texture = canvas.texture(crop); // photo cropped to cover the viewport

const MODES = [
  { id: 'swirl', chain: ({ x, y, r, k, spin }) => [['swirl', x, y, r, k * (2.4 + spin)], ['vignette', 0.3, 0.45 * k]] },
  { id: 'halftone', chain: ({ x, y, r, k, s }) => [['colorHalftone', x, y, 0.25, (1 + 2.6 * k) * s], ['bulgePinch', x, y, r, 0.8 * k]] },
];

let c = canvas.draw(texture);
for (const [fn, ...args] of ops) c = c[fn](...args);
c.update();

reglIridescent feedback puddle

Functional, stateless WebGL with declarative draw commands

regl turns WebGL into plain functions: a framebuffer pair and two draw commands give you a ping-pong video-feedback loop in a few lines. Each frame displaces the previous one along curl noise and your pointer, runs a convolution kernel, hue-rotates it, then lights the result as a thin-film oil slick. Built in the spirit of Ezra Miller's iridescentpuddle.com.

npm i regl
const fbos = [makeFbo(w, h), makeFbo(w, h)];
const step = regl({
  frag: FEEDBACK_GLSL, vert, attributes: quad, count: 3,
  uniforms: { prev: regl.prop('src'), t: regl.prop('t'), kmode: regl.prop('k') },
  framebuffer: regl.prop('dst'),
});
regl.frame(() => {
  step({ src: fbos[cur], dst: fbos[1 - cur], t, k: kernel }); cur = 1 - cur;
  show({ src: fbos[cur], phase: palette.phase });
});

glitch-canvasJPEG-corrupted broadcast

Glitches images by corrupting their JPEG bytes

glitch-canvas does not fake glitches with filters: it encodes the image as JPEG, overwrites bytes in the compressed stream (amount, iterations, seed, quality), and decodes whatever survives.   seed: (seedBase + frame) % 100,
  quality: Math.round(92 - intensity * 70),
  amount: Math.round(2 + intensity * 60),
  iterations: Math.round(1 + intensity * 18),
})
  .fromImageData(sctx.getImageData(0, 0, W, H))
  .toImageData();
octx.putImageData(img, 0, 0);

  wave.setAmplitude(amp);

gpu-ioPhysarum slime-mold network

GPGPU toolkit for WebGL physics and simulations

Amanda Ghassaei's gpu-io wraps WebGL1/2 in layers and fragment-shader programs, so a simulation is a few step() calls instead of framebuffer plumbing. Here 128k–1.2M agents (scaled to the GPU) sense, turn and deposit chemoattractant in float textures, building a living transport network you can lure or scatter with the cursor.

npm i gpu-io
const trail = new GPULayer(composer, { name: 'trail', dimensions: [w, h],
  numComponents: 1, type: FLOAT, filter: LINEAR, numBuffers: 2, wrapX: REPEAT, wrapY: REPEAT });

composer.step({ program: updateParticles,
  input: [particlesHeading, particlesPositions, trail],
  output: [particlesHeading, particlesPositions] });
composer.drawLayerAsPoints({ layer: particlesPositions, program: deposit,
  input: trail, output: trail, pointSize: 1, wrapX: true, wrapY: true });
composer.step({ program: diffuseAndDecay, input: trail, output: trail });
composer.step({ program: render, input: trail });

HeerichCarvable voxel sculpture

Tiny engine for voxel scenes rendered as crisp SVG

meodai's Heerich builds voxel scenes with boolean ops (union, subtract, intersect, exclude) and paints every face from a style map, including the walls a subtraction exposes, then outputs plain SVG polygons with no canvas or WebGL. This sculpture after Erwin Heerich can be carved, drilled and added to by tapping faces (hit-tested with findByPosition). It switches live between oblique, isometric, orthographic and perspective cameras, and three palettes restyle every face.

npm i heerich
h.applyGeometry({ type: 'box', position: [-4, -7, -4], size: [9, 7, 9],
  style: { x: { fill: P.x }, z: { fill: P.z },
    top: (x, y) => ({ fill: mix(P.top, '#ffffff', Math.min(1, -y / 14) * 0.6) }) } });
// carve: custom 'fill' sphere; style paints the newly exposed walls
h.applyGeometry({ type: 'fill', mode: 'subtract', bounds,
  test: (x, y, z) => y < 0 && (x - c[0]) ** 2 + (y - c[1]) ** 2 + (z - c[2]) ** 2 <= r * r,
  style: { default: { fill: P.wall, hatch: { angle: 45, period: 5, stroke: P.hatch } } } });
h.setCamera({ type: 'isometric', angle: 45 + t * 11 });
const hit = h.findByPosition([x, y]); // tap -> { voxel, face }
stage.innerHTML = h.toSVG({ faces, viewBox });

Leon SansKinetic type playground

A geometric sans typeface made entirely of code

Jongmin Kim's Leon Sans has no font file. Every glyph is stored as stroke coordinates, so canvas code can change the weight smoothly from 1 to 900, draw the letters stroke by stroke, or turn them into waves, patterns and plants. This playground runs the library's own effects (drawing, wave(), pattern(), the colour-pattern example) on any text you type. A plants mode grows leaves along the glyph paths.

  align: 'center', isWave: true, pathGap: 0.3, amplitude: 0.5, fps: 30 });
leon.position(r.x + (r.w - leon.rect.w) / 2, r.y + (r.h - leon.rect.h) / 2);
// drawing animation: tween every glyph's drawing value 0 -> 1
for (let i = 0; i < d.length; i++) d[i].value = ease4(t);
if (m === 'draw') leon.draw(ctx);
else if (m === 'wave') leon.wave(ctx, now);
else if (m === 'pattern') leon.pattern(ctx, +$weight.value, ph);

bouffontGraffiti wall lettering

Generative puffy lettering grown from any font, as SVG

bouffont reduces every glyph of a font to its centre lines, redraws them with one pen, then grows them with a chain of strategies: inflate, block, pack, coral or DLA growth, plus outer bands, shine and 3D effects. Every part is tagged with data-part, so this demo styles the plain black-and-white output into graffiti with CSS alone (gradient fills, band colour, stepped drop shadows) and plays bouffontLive() step by step so each piece visibly grows. It's seeded and deterministic, and the letters are Rubik (OFL), loaded from a local WOFF.

npm i bouffont
import rubikUrl from '@fontsource/rubik/files/rubik-latin-400-normal.woff?url';
import { bouffontLive, drawFrame, loadFont } from 'bouffont';

const font = await loadFont(rubikUrl); // TTF/OTF/WOFF (not WOFF2)
const live = bouffontLive({ text: 'BOUFFONT', font, seed, preset: 'throwup',
  render: { outline: 0.5 }, effects: [['shine', { angle: 225 }]] });
while (live.step()) {
  const fr = live.frame();
  el.innerHTML = drawFrame({ ...fr, render: { ...fr.render, draft: true } }).svg;
  await nextFrame();
}
el.innerHTML = live.final().svg; // [data-part="fill"], [data-part="band"]… styled by CSS

Heptapod InkInk logograms that read back

Arrival-style circular ink logograms from text, and back again

Heptapod Ink packs a phrase into one large number with a CRC-16 checksum and draws each digit as a swelling or tendril on a single brush-ink ring, as plain SVG. The demo reveals each ring clockwise from its gap, eases the library's own displacement filter from wet to settled, then runs decode() on the SVG markup in the DOM and types the text back. Tapping the ring changes the seed: the ink looks different, but it decodes to the same message.

npm i heptapod-ink
import { encode, decode } from 'heptapod-ink';

const res = encode(text, { seed });          // { svg, slots, radius, size, checksum, compact }
inkBox.innerHTML = res.svg;
const svg = inkBox.firstElementChild;
svg.querySelector('g').setAttribute('mask', 'url(#sweep)'); // clockwise reveal from the gap

// later: read it back from what is on screen
const { text: out } = decode(svg.outerHTML);

Matt DesLauriers' framework for print-sized generative art

let a = rnd.noise2D(x, y, freq) * Math.PI * turns;

@thi.ng/geom-fuzzBoiling isometric sketch

Fuzzy, hand-drawn lines and polygons with composable hatch fills

Karsten Schmidt's geom-fuzz turns clean @thi.ng/geom shapes into wobbly, overshooting pen strokes, and its fills (hatch, dots, marker-pen) compose like functions, so one compFill() call stacks crosshatch layers. Here a seeded isometric town is shaded face by face with six pen presets built only from those primitives. The outlines 'boil' by cycling a few fresh jitter passes, the way hand-drawn animation does.

npm i @thi.ng/geom-fuzz @thi.ng/geom @thi.ng/hiccup-canvas
const hatch = (dir, space, a, flip) => defHatch({ dir, flip, space,
  line: { jitter: 0.7, resample: 3, attribs: { stroke: g(a), weight: 0.7 } } });
// pencil preset: fills compose like functions
left: hatch('d', s * 1.15, 0.42),
right: compFill(hatch('d', s * 0.8, 0.5), hatch('d', s * 1.1, 0.4, 'x')),
// ink preset: the library's marker-pen hatch
right: defHatchPen(ink, 'd', t, (s * 0.62) / t, 3),
// every face: fuzzy outline passes + its fill, drawn via hiccup-canvas
out.push(fuzzyPoly(pts, { ...P.edge.attribs, fill: 'none' }, {
  num: P.edge.passes, jitter: P.edge.jitter, curve: { scale: P.edge.curve }, fill }));
draw(ctx, ['g', { lineCap: 'round', lineJoin: 'round' }, ...out]);

PenroseEuler diagrams that solve themselves

Type math notation, get a diagram laid out by optimization

CMU's Penrose splits a diagram into Domain (types), Substance (what is true) and Style (how to draw it), then finds a layout by numerically minimising constraint energy. Here you edit the Substance live and watch the optimizer's real trajectory replayed, with the energy curve drawn alongside. Drag a set and Penrose solves again from where you dropped it.

res = await P.compile({
  domain,
  style: style(...canvasWH),
  substance: ta.value,
  variation: variation(),
});
const r = P.stepTimes(s, 1); // one optimizer step, kept for playback
s = r.value;
snaps.push({ vv: vv.slice(), L, e: P.evalEnergy(s) });
const svg = await P.toSVG({ ...cur, varyingValues: v }, noImports, 'pz');
// drag a set, release, and Penrose re-solves from there
dispVV = P.translateVaryingValues(drag.path, dx, dy, drag.vv0, drag.vv0, cur);

MarkovJunior WebWorlds grown from rewrite rules

TypeScript port of the MarkovJunior probabilistic rewrite-rule language

Yuu6883's browser port of mxgmn's MarkovJunior (MIT), a language where a program is an XML tree of pattern rewrites like WBB → WAW, applied at random until nothing matches. Eight models from the repo (rivers, flowers, dungeons, islands, a lost city) grow on the real interpreter here. The node that is firing is lit up in its XML source, and its in → out patterns are drawn in the model's palette.

git clone https://github.com/Yuu6883/MarkovJuniorWeb && cp -r MarkovJuniorWeb/src vendor/markovjunior-web/
const doc = Loader.xmlParse(MODEL_SRC[name]);
const ip = await Interpreter.load(doc, N, N, 1);
cur = { ip, it: ip.run(seed, steps) /* generator */ };
// every animation frame: advance k rewrite steps, then paint
for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) {
  if (cur.it.next().done) { cur.done = true; break; }
}
const [state] = ip.state(); // Uint8Array of symbol indices
const node = activeNode(cur.ip); // the node that is firing
const ln = cur.lineOf.get(node.source); // its XML element -> line

Spectral.jsWet paint, two mixing models

Kubelka-Munk pigment mixing for the web

Spectral.js turns each colour into a reflectance curve and mixes the curves with Kubelka-Munk theory, so blue and yellow make green the way paint does instead of averaging to grey. The demo is a smudgy brush simulation. One painting is rendered twice, spectral on one side of the slider and plain RGB averaging on the other, so the same strokes show both results.

npm i spectral.js
const pig = PIGMENTS.map((p) => new Color(p.hex));
const paper = new Color(PAPER_HEX);
// per paint cell: quantized pigment amounts -> Kubelka-Munk mix
for (let k = 0; k <= K; k++) {
  const q = qa[k];
  if (!q) continue;
  const c = k < K ? pig[k] : paper;
  pairs.push([c, q]);
}
[sr, sg, sb] = mix(...pairs).sRGB;

p5.grain applies the analog finish that generative prints usually get in post: per-pixel monochromatic or chromatic grain, tiled paper textures blended onto the canvas, and a tinkerPixels loop for custom pixel passes. Here a three-ink riso poster runs through all three on a sheet-sized p5.Graphics buffer, using a seeded random so the grain is deterministic. Drag the wipe to compare it with the clean render.

p5grain.setup({ instance: p, ignoreWarnings: true });

proc.image(art, -paperRect.x, -paperRect.y);
p5grain.tinkerPixels((i) => {          // ink dropout
  if (px === null) px = proc.pixels;
  const mv = mask[i >> 2];
  if (mv <= thr - soft) return;
  const k = Math.min(1, (mv - thr + soft) / (soft * 2));
  px[i] += (PAPER[0] - px[i]) * k; // …g, b
}, true, proc);
p5grain.applyMonochromaticGrain(state.grain, false, proc);
p5grain.textureOverlay(textures[state.paper], { mode: p.MULTIPLY, animate: { atFrame: 1, amount: 256 } }, proc);

Palettes interpolated between anchor colours along polar HSL paths

meodai's Poline puts colours on a polar wheel, with hue as the angle and lightness as the radius, then interpolates between anchor points. A separate position function eases each axis, so the same anchors give very different ramps under sinusoidal, exponential or arc. This demo uses Poline's own <poline-picker> web component: drag the anchors and the Bauhaus tile poster and swatch strip recolour live. The hue drifts slowly when idle.

import { Poline, positionFunctions } from 'poline/picker';

const poline = new Poline({
  anchorColors: [[318, .82, .84], [12, .9, .56], [204, .78, .22]],
  numPoints: 5,
  positionFunction: positionFunctions.sinusoidalPosition,
});
picker.setPoline(poline);               // <poline-picker interactive>
picker.addEventListener('poline-change', redraw);
poline.invertedLightness = true;  poline.closedLoop = true;
poline.shiftHue(0.22);                   // idle drift
const palette = poline.colors;          // [[h, s, l], …]

Procedural house plants drawn as SVG in fineliner and watercolour

Orta Therox's generator grows 52 species from a seed and draws them with broken hand-length pen strokes, off-register watercolour washes and paper knockouts, returning a plain SVG string with no DOM and no dependencies. Age is not a scale factor: as it rises, leaf count, fenestration, crown spread and pot wear all change, so the growth animation here shows a monstera's blades splitting as it matures. Tap a pot to sow a new seed, or swap the palette and the paper changes with it.

npm i @orta/sketchy-plants
import { drawPlant, species, palettes } from '@orta/sketchy-plants';

const recipe = { ...species[s.kind], palette: palettes[palette] };
const a = Math.max(1, Math.round(s.age)); // animated 1 → age to grow it
s.art.innerHTML = drawPlant({
  seed: s.seed, recipe, age: a,
  relativeSize: true, // frame sized for the grown plant: it grows in place
  margin: 8, idPrefix: `p${slots.indexOf(s)}`,
});
// washes knock out to the palette's paper, so the page must match it
document.documentElement.style.setProperty('--paper', P.paper);

Each figure is a filled-plate isometric line drawing (a keyboard, a vault, a commit graph) that does one physical thing when the pointer arrives: a key sinks, a dial turns, a drawer slides out. npm i @lucasmarkes/hairline

const fig = H[name](host, {
  intensity,
  play: true, // the library's own ghost pointer walks each figure while idle
  theme: document.body.dataset.style === 'vellum' ? 'light' : 'dark',
  onRead: (t) => { ro.textContent = t.replace(/ · /g, '·'); ro.title = t; },
});
// intensity slider
live.forEach(({ fig }) => fig.update({ intensity }));
/* style.css: five custom properties theme every figure */
--hairline-plate: #0c0d0f; --hairline-hi: #f2bd5c; --hairline-edge: #b9bbc1;

Three.js globe component for arcs, hexbins, rings and labels

d3-voronoi-treemapMorphing world economy

D3 plugin computing treemaps from weighted Voronoi tessellations

Instead of rectangles, cells are weighted Voronoi polygons inside any convex shape, which gives hierarchical data an organic, cell-like look. Countries nest inside continents within a circle, and the cells morph between GDP (PPP) and population shares. Data: Natural Earth (public domain).

npm i d3-voronoi-treemap
const root = d3.hierarchy(data).sum(d => d.children ? 0 : d[metric])
voronoiTreemap()
  .clip(circlePolygon)
  .prng(d3.randomLcg(0.42))
  .convergenceRatio(0.005)
  .maxIterationCount(60)
  .minWeightRatio(0.002)(root)
root.leaves().forEach(l => draw(l.polygon, l.data))

Rough.jsBoiling sketchbook landscape

Draw shapes that look hand-sketched, on canvas or SVG

Rough.js turns any rectangle, ellipse, polygon or SVG path into wobbly, hand-drawn strokes with hachure, cross-hatch, zigzag or dot fills. A seed makes each sketch reproducible, so cycling through three seeds gives the 'line boil' of hand-drawn animation. At under 9 kB gzipped, it powers Excalidraw-style UIs and wired-elements.

npm i roughjs
const rc = rough.canvas(canvas);
const o = (i, extra = {}) => ({
  roughness: state.roughness, bowing: state.bowing, seed: seedBase * 97 + i,
  stroke: C.ink, fillStyle: state.fillStyle, hachureGap: 7, ...extra,
});
rc.rectangle(360, 300, 230, 145, o(i++, { fill: C.coral }));
rc.polygon([[340, 305], [475, 205], [610, 305]], o(i++, { fill: C.violet }));
rc.circle(702, 285, 130, o(i++, { fill: C.green }));
rc.curve(tail, o(i++, { stroke: C.amber }));

perfect-freehandPressure-sensitive ink pad

Turns pointer points into smooth, pressure-sensitive ink outlines

perfect-freehand takes raw pointer samples and returns the outline polygon of a variable-width stroke, simulating pressure from speed when there is no stylus.   end: { taper: size * 5, cap: true },
});
path.setAttribute('d', getSvgPathFromStroke(outline));

VivusLighthouse that draws itself

Animates SVG strokes so illustrations appear to draw themselves

Vivus animates stroke-dashoffset on every path of an inline SVG, so line art appears to be drawn by hand. It has three timing modes (delayed, sync, oneByOne), separate easing per path and for the whole timeline, and setFrameProgress() for scrubbing or scroll-linking. It has no dependencies and works on any SVG you already have.

npm i vivus
viv = new Vivus(svg, {
  type: 'oneByOne', start: 'manual', duration: 260,
  animTimingFunction: Vivus.EASE,
  pathTimingFunction: Vivus.EASE_OUT_BOUNCE,
});
viv.play(1, () => svg.classList.add('done'));   // draw
viv.play(-4, () => setTimeout(draw, 500));        // rewind
scrub.oninput = () => viv.stop().setFrameProgress(+scrub.value);

MotionInterruptible spring field

Production animation library for JS, React and Vue

Motion's vanilla animate() drives real spring physics through hardware-accelerated transforms, and re-targeting a running spring keeps its velocity, so a tile pushed mid-bounce never snaps. Function-valued delays and stagger() turn one call into a grid-wide ripple; press() adds tactile gestures without a framework.

npm i motion
// re-target on every pointer move — velocity carries over
animate(cell, { x: tx, y: ty, scale: s, rotate: rot },
  { type: spring, stiffness: 320, damping: 14, mass: 0.8 });

// grid ripple: delay is any function of the index
animate(tiles, { y: [0, -size * 0.45, 0], rotate: [r0, rotAcc] },
  { duration: 0.6, ease: [0.22, 1, 0.36, 1], delay: (i) => dist[i] * 0.05 });

press(grid, (target) => {
  animate(tile, { scale: 0.7 }, { type: spring, visualDuration: 0.2, bounce: 0.2 });
  return () => ripple(+cell.dataset.i);
});

  stagger: 0.025, absolute: true, nested: true });

Draggable.create(cards(), {
  type: 'x,y', bounds: '#stage', inertia: true, edgeResistance: 0.8,
  onThrowComplete() { home(this.target); },
});

Matter.jsThrowable gravity type

2D rigid-body physics engine for the web

Matter.js handles collisions, friction, restitution, sleeping bodies and mouse constraints, and leaves rendering to you, so physics can look like type and UI instead of debug wireframes. Here every letter and pill is a chamfered rigid body drawn on a custom canvas renderer.

npm i matter-js
const engine = Engine.create({ enableSleeping: true });
const b = Bodies.rectangle(x, y, S * 0.92, S * 1.08, {
  chamfer: { radius: S * 0.16 }, restitution: 0.25, friction: 0.6,
});
Composite.add(engine.world, b);

const mouse = Mouse.create(canvas);
Composite.add(engine.world, MouseConstraint.create(engine, {
  mouse, constraint: { stiffness: 0.18, damping: 0.08 },
}));
Engine.update(engine, 1000 / 60);   // then draw bodies yourself

LenisSilk-smooth parallax scroll

Smooth scroll that keeps native scrolling semantics

Lenis interpolates the wheel/trackpad input while the page keeps its real scrollbar, position: sticky and anchor links. Its scroll event exposes eased scroll, velocity and progress every frame, enough to drive parallax layers, velocity-skewed marquees and progress bars from one listener.

npm i lenis
const lenis = new Lenis({ lerp: 0.08, autoRaf: true });

lenis.on('scroll', ({ scroll, velocity, progress }) => {
  const mid = scroll + innerHeight / 2;
  layers.forEach((el, i) => {
    el.style.transform = `translate3d(0, ${((mid - base[i]) * +el.dataset.speed).toFixed(1)}px, 0)`;
  });
  skew += (Math.max(-12, Math.min(12, velocity * 0.6)) - skew) * 0.2;
  bar.style.transform = `scaleX(${progress})`;
});

lenis.scrollTo(0, { duration: 2.2 });

.pupil      { --k-follow: 1; --k-limit: 4px; --k-area: viewport; }
.plane      { --k-follow: .9; --k-point: 90deg; }

flubberSplit-and-merge silhouettes

Best-guess interpolation between arbitrary SVG shapes

flubber morphs between shapes with different point counts and topology: it resamples both outlines, finds the best rotation to align them, and triangulates a shape to split it into many (separate) or fuse many into one (combine). Here a fish breaks into a school of seven, the school merges into a bird, and a moon scatters into stars. Each step is a plain t → path function driven by a hand-rolled rAF tween.

npm i flubber
function build(from, toState) {
  const to = toState.shapes;
  if (from.length === 1 && to.length === 1) return { fn: 'interpolate', fns: [interpolate(from[0], to[0], OPTS)] };
  if (from.length === 1) return { fn: 'separate', fns: separate(from[0], to, OPTS) };
  if (to.length === 1) return { fn: 'combine', fns: combine(from, to[0], OPTS) };
  if (from.length === to.length) return { fn: 'interpolateAll', fns: interpolateAll(from, to, OPTS) };
  return { fn: 'combine', fns: combine(from, to[0], OPTS) };
}
const strings = morph.fns.map((f, i) => {
  const local = Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (raw - morph.stagger * i) / span));
  return f(n > 1 ? easeSoft(local) : ease(local));
});

KUTE.jsCubic-morphing glyph chain

Tween engine with SVG cubic morph, draw and text-write components

KUTE.js tweens things CSS can't: svgCubicMorph converts two unrelated paths to cubic béziers, splits them to equal segment counts and picks the rotation with the least travel, svgDraw animates stroke length, and textWrite scrambles text into place character by character. Here a chain of seven glyphs morphs with lagging outline echoes, a drawn progress ring, a type-written label and a matrix-based 3D sway, all as plain KUTE tweens from its 'extra' build.

npm i kute.js
import KUTE from 'kute.js/src/index-extra.js'; // svgCubicMorph build
const morphOpts = { duration: MORPH, easing: 'easingCubicInOut' };
live = [
  KUTE.to(shape, { path: d }, morphOpts),
  KUTE.to(echo, { path: d }, { ...morphOpts, delay: 140 }),
  KUTE.fromTo('#ring', { draw: '0% 0%' }, { draw: '0% 100%' }, { duration: MORPH + HOLD, easing: 'linear' }),
  KUTE.fromTo('#glyph', { transform: { scale3d: [0.9, 0.9, 1] } }, { transform: { scale3d: [1, 1, 1] } }, { duration: 800, easing: 'easingBackOut' }),
  KUTE.to('#name', { text: name }, { duration: 560, textChars: 'alpha' }),
];
live.forEach((t) => t.start());

Motion CanvasUnwinding a circle into a wave

Code-driven animation: generators, signals and tweens on canvas

Scenes are TypeScript generators: every yield* is a tween, and nodes bind straight to reactive signals, so labels and diagrams update with the values they show. Its Code node morphs one snippet into the next token by token, which is what makes its 3Blue1Brown-style explainers look the way they do.

npm i @motion-canvas/core @motion-canvas/2d
return makeScene2D(function* (view) {
    const angle = createSignal(0);
    const terms = createSignal(1);
      yield* all(code.code(S3, 1.0), code.selection(lines(1, 5), 0.6), four(1, 0.8));
      yield* terms(3, 2.4, easeInOutCubic);
    yield* all(angle(TAU * 6, DURATION, linear), story());

interact.jsInertia corkboard

Drag, resize and multi-touch gestures with inertia and snapping

interact.js gives you raw pointer physics rather than a drag-and-drop widget: throws keep their momentum and glide to a stop, modifiers snap to a grid or clamp to the parent, and two-finger gestures report rotation and scale. It only reports deltas and leaves rendering to you, so the transforms here are plain CSS variables.

npm i interactjs
interact(el).draggable({
  inertia: { resistance: 7, minSpeed: 120, endSpeed: 20 },
  modifiers: snapOn ? [restrict, snapModifier()] : [restrict],
  listeners: { move(e) { const s = state.get(e.target); s.x += e.dx; s.y += e.dy; apply(e.target); } },
});
// restrict = interact.modifiers.restrictRect({ restriction: 'parent', endOnly: true })
// snapModifier = interact.modifiers.snap({ targets: [interact.snappers.grid({ x, y })], endOnly: true })
interact(el).resizable({ edges: { right: '.grip', bottom: '.grip' } });
interact(el).gesturable({ listeners: { move(e) { s.r += e.da; apply(el); } } });

AnimXYZComposable entrance mixer

Compose CSS animations from xyz utility attributes and variables

AnimXYZ builds animations from words: an xyz="fade small rotate-right stagger-0.5" attribute sets CSS variables, and a single shared keyframe combines them, so effects stack without writing @keyframes. Stagger reads a per-element --xyz-index, which drives the diagonal sweep here. Toggle the chips to mix your own.

npm i @animxyz/core
import '@animxyz/core';

grid.setAttribute('xyz', 'fade small rotate-right stagger-0.5 ease-out-back');
// AnimXYZ's stagger reads --xyz-index: diagonal sweep
tiles.forEach((el, i) => el.style.setProperty('--xyz-index', (i % cols) + Math.floor(i / cols)));
tiles.forEach((t) => t.classList.add('xyz-out'));   // exit
t.classList.remove('xyz-out'); void t.offsetWidth; t.classList.add('xyz-in');   // re-enter

smooothyVelocity-skew infinite strip

Tiny bring-your-own-effects smooth slider core

smooothy is a small lerped slider core: you call update() in your own loop and read current, parallaxValues and deltaTime to build the effects yourself. Here the measured speed is smoothed with its own damp() and drives skew, squash, a colour trail and a background marquee across twelve canvas-painted landscapes, with idle auto-drift surges so it never stands still.

npm i smooothy
const slider = new Core(strip, { infinite: true, snap: true, lerpFactor: 0.22, scrollInput: true });
function frame(now) {
  slider.update();
  const vel = (slider.current - prevCurrent) / dt; prevCurrent = slider.current;
  lv = damp(lv, clamp(vel, -12, 12), 7, dt);
  const skew = clamp(lv * 6.5, -22, 22);
  cards.forEach((card, i) => {
    const p = slider.parallaxValues[i], dist = Math.min(Math.abs(p), 2.5);
    card.style.transform = `skewX(${skew}deg) scale(${1 - dist * 0.07})`;
  });
}

mo.jsBurst garden + like heart

Declarative motion-graphics toolbelt: bursts, swirls and shape primitives

mo.js ships SVG motion primitives (Shape, ShapeSwirl, Burst) instead of a generic tween API: you declare a burst of zigzags, crosses and curves with property maps and it choreographs the whole explosion. This garden pools 14 layered bursts and replays them with .tune({x, y}).replay(), so the DOM never grows, around the classic mo.js like-heart burst.

npm i @mojs/core
const shapes = new mojs.Burst({
  parent: fx, left: 0, top: 0,
  radius: { [R * 0.12]: R }, count: 14, angle: { 0: 40 },
  children: {
    shape: ["circle", "polygon", "zigzag", "cross", "curve", "rect"],
    angle: { 0: "rand(-260, 260)" }, scale: { 1: 0, easing: "quad.in" },
    duration: "rand(2200, 2800)", easing: "cubic.out",
  },
});
// pooled: replay at the tap point instead of creating new DOM
g.shapes.tune({ x, y }).generate().replay();

pushIn.jsNight transit dolly

Scroll-driven camera dolly that pushes layers past the viewer

pushIn.js turns page scroll into a camera dolly: stacked layers scale up from the vanishing point and fade out as they pass you, each with its own in/out scroll points, speed and fade lengths. Plain HTML plus data attributes, no WebGL and no framework, so typographic and SVG art stays crisp at any zoom.

npm i pushin
plan.forEach((p, i) => {
  const d = layers[i].dataset;   // .pushin-layer elements
  d.pushinFrom = p.from;           // scroll px where the layer starts
  d.pushinTo = p.to;               // ...and where it leaves
  d.pushinSpeed = p.speed;         // how fast it grows
  if (p.tStart) d.pushinTransitionStart = p.tStart;
  if (p.tEnd) d.pushinTransitionEnd = p.tEnd;
});
const pin = new PushIn(document.getElementById('pin'), { mode: 'sequential', autoStart: 'scroll' });
pin.start();

It updates DOM styles through progress subscriptions instead of re-rendering React each frame, and ships HorizontalScroll, Parallax, Progress and Marquee in the same package.

npm i react-kino
<Kino>
  <Scene duration="320vh">
    <TextReveal at={0.04} span={0.5} dimColor="rgba(246,239,230,.34)">
      A pocket moon of hand-blown glass, held by three rings that never stop turning.
    </TextReveal>
    <ScrollTransform perspective={900} easing="ease-in-out-cubic"
      from={{ rotateX: 58, rotateY: -28, scale: 0.62, y: 30 }}
      to={{ rotateX: -8, rotateY: 24, scale: 1.08, y: 0 }}>
      <Halo />
    </ScrollTransform>
  </Scene>
  <Scene duration="240vh"><Counter from={0} to={1800} at={0.08} span={0.45} /></Scene>
  <HorizontalScroll>{MODES.map((m) => <Panel key={m.n}>…</Panel>)}</HorizontalScroll>
</Kino>

Drop-in clip-path transitions triggered by one HTML attribute

npm i transition-style
import 'transition-style'; // all 52 clip-path presets
// style.css → :root { --transition__duration: 1.3s; }

// 'in': the new poster lands on top and reveals itself
stage.append(next);
next.setAttribute('transition-style', 'in:circle:hesitate');

// 'out': the new poster goes underneath, the old one clips away
stage.insertBefore(next, outgoing);
outgoing.setAttribute('transition-style', 'out:wipe:right');
// on animationend: remove old poster + attribute, ready for the next

Peel.jsPeelable die-cut sticker sheet

Corner-peel effect for HTML elements using SVG clip paths

Peel.js splits an element into top, back and bottom layers, clips them along a moving fold line with SVG clip paths, and adds shadows and a back-side reflection, so plain HTML peels like a real sticker or page corner. Shapes can be circles, polygons or any SVG path (this sheet has a heart, a starburst and a ticket), and you can tween the peel along a bezier path with setPeelPath and setTimeAlongPath.

curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andrewplummer/peel-js/master/src/peel.js

  corner: Peel.Corners.TOP_LEFT,

  backReflection: true, backShadowAlpha: 0.18,
});
// drag: drive the corner with pointer events
peel.setPeelPosition(p.x + off.x, p.y + off.y);
// idle / exit: tween along a bezier and fade out
peel.setFadeThreshold(0.55);
peel.setPeelPath(a.x, a.y, c.x, c.y, c.x, c.y, b.x, b.y);
peel.setTimeAlongPath(ease(k));

SwupFour themes, one mini-site

Page transitions for server-rendered multi-page sites

Swup intercepts links, fetches the next real HTML page and swaps only the container, with CSS classes timing each phase so the transition itself stays plain CSS. This three-page site switches live between the official overlay, slide and fade themes and the parallel plugin, which keeps the old and new pages on screen at the same time.

npm i swup @swup/overlay-theme @swup/slide-theme @swup/fade-theme @swup/parallel-plugin
const swup = new Swup({ containers: ['#swup'] });

function setMode(m) {
  if (plugin) swup.unuse(plugin);
  plugin = {
    overlay: () => new SwupOverlayTheme({ color: '#f1c96b' }),
    slide: () => new SwupSlideTheme(),
    fade: () => new SwupFadeTheme(),
    parallel: () => new SwupParallelPlugin({ containers: ['#swup'] }),
  }[m]();
  swup.use(plugin);
}

lax.jsSpeed-reactive type poster

Tiny scroll animation library driven by position and velocity

lax.js binds any CSS property to a driver value through keyframe arrays, and its drivers can track inertia, a smoothed scroll velocity. That makes speed itself a design input: headlines shear, blur and track out the faster you scroll, while shapes and marquees stay locked to position.

npm i lax.js
lax.init();
lax.addDriver('scrollY', () => window.scrollY, { inertiaEnabled: true });

lax.addElements('.l1', {
  scrollY: {
    skewX: [[0], [0], { inertia: 1.8, cssFn: clamp(-34, 34) }],
    blur: [[0], [0], { inertia: 0.2, inertiaMode: 'absolute', cssFn: clamp(0, 6) }],
    'letter-spacing': [[0], [0], { inertia: 1, inertiaMode: 'absolute',
      cssFn: (v) => `${(-0.03 + Math.min(+v, 30) * 0.011).toFixed(3)}em` }],
  },
});

Google's Box2D particle-fluid fork, compiled to WebAssembly

LiquidFun adds a particle solver to Box2D: water, viscous, elastic and rigid particle groups that collide with ordinary rigid bodies. gd.shape = shape;
const g = ps.CreateParticleGroup(gd);
world.Step(dt, 6, 2, 3);

Jolt PhysicsCannonball tower demolition

The AAA rigid-body engine behind Horizon Forbidden West, in WASM

JoltPhysics.js compiles Jorrit Rouwe's C++ engine to WebAssembly and exposes nearly its full API: layer filters, body interfaces, CCD, sleeping islands. Here a few hundred interlocking bricks stack stably, get smashed by dense continuous-collision cannonballs, then fly back home on a loop. The single-thread .wasm build is about 2 MB and needs no COOP/COEP headers.

npm i jolt-physics
const Jolt = await initJolt({ locateFile: () => wasmUrl });
const jolt = new Jolt.JoltInterface(settings);
const physics = jolt.GetPhysicsSystem();
const bi = physics.GetBodyInterface();
const brickShape = new Jolt.BoxShape(brickHe, 0.03, null);
const cs = new Jolt.BodyCreationSettings(brickShape, tR, tQ, Jolt.EMotionType_Dynamic, LAYER_MOVING);
const body = bi.CreateBody(cs);
bi.AddBody(body.GetID(), Jolt.EActivation_Activate);
// each frame:
jolt.Step(dt, dt > 1 / 22 ? 4 : dt > 1 / 35 ? 3 : dt > 1 / 55 ? 2 : 1);

planck.jsBlueprint joint machines

Box2D rewritten in TypeScript: rigid bodies, joints, motors

A faithful Box2D port that gives you the engine's real joint toolkit: wheel joints with spring suspension and motors, revolute chains, mouse joints, reaction forces you can read every step. Here a motorised car drives an endless procedural course of breakable rope bridges, crate stacks and a Newton's cradle, drawn as a live engineering drawing.

npm i planck
const w = world.createBody({ type: "dynamic", position: car.getWorldPoint(WL[k]), angularDamping: 0.1 });
w.createFixture({ shape: new Circle(WHEEL_R), density: 1.3, friction: 0.95 });
springs.push(world.createJoint(new WheelJoint({ motorSpeed: 0, maxMotorTorque: k ? 20 : 32,
  enableMotor: true, frequencyHz: 4.2, dampingRatio: 0.7 }, car, w, w.getPosition(), Vec2(0, 1))));

// each step: drive the motors, snap overloaded bridge pins
springs.forEach((s) => s.setMotorSpeed(-speed));
if (j.getReactionForce(1 / dt).length() > BREAK) { world.destroyJoint(j); J[k] = null; }

// pointer: drag any body
new MouseJoint({ maxForce: mass * 260, frequencyHz: 5, dampingRatio: 0.7 }, mouseGround, body, Vec2(p.x, p.y));

cannon-esLacquered domino spiral

Lightweight 3D rigid-body physics engine in plain JavaScript

The pmndrs-maintained ES-module fork of cannon.js: boxes, spheres, contact materials, impulses and sleeping in a tree-shakable package that pairs naturally with three.js. Here 107 box bodies with tuned contact materials carry a real chain reaction through a spiral, then rewind and run again.

npm i cannon-es
const world = new CANNON.World({ gravity: new CANNON.Vec3(0, -70, 0), allowSleep: true });
world.broadphase = new CANNON.SAPBroadphase(world);
const stiff = { contactEquationRelaxation: 1, frictionEquationRelaxation: 1 };
world.addContactMaterial(new CANNON.ContactMaterial(mDomino, mDomino, { friction: 0.12, restitution: 0.6, ...stiff }));
const body = new CANNON.Body({
  mass: 1, material: mDomino, shape: new CANNON.Box(new CANNON.Vec3(W / 2, H / 2, T / 2)),
  allowSleep: false, linearDamping: 0.01, angularDamping: 0.03,
});
// tap a domino: flick it along the spiral's tangent
tmpV.set(d.tx * strength, 0, d.tz * strength);
d.body.applyImpulse(tmpV, tmpP);
world.step(1 / 60);

verlet-jsDewy night spider web

Tiny 2D Verlet engine: particles, distance, pin and angle constraints

verlet-js is the 2013 engine behind the famous canvas spiderweb and cloth demos: everything is particles joined by distance constraints, relaxed a few times per frame. Here an orb web (spokes, a real capture spiral, sagging anchor chains) is built from raw Particles and DistanceConstraints; a spider walks the live constraint graph and its weight dents the silk. Drag uses the engine's own nearestEntity()/draggedEntity, and overstretched or swiped strands are simply removed from the composite.

git clone https://github.com/subprotocol/verlet-js (use js/verlet-1.0.0.js)
world = new VerletJS(W, H, canvas);
const comp = new world.Composite();
const add = (x, y) => { const p = new Particle(new Vec2(x, y)); P.push(p); return p; };
const c = new DistanceConstraint(a, b, type === 'spiral' ? 0.55 : 0.8);
c.distance *= tensor; // pre-tension the silk
const pin = comp.pin(P.length - 1); // tie a thread to the branch
// pointer: let verlet-js pick the nearest particle or pin
world.mouse.x = p.x; world.mouse.y = p.y;
const ent = world.nearestEntity();
if (ent) world.draggedEntity = ent;
world.frame(STEPS); // integrate + relax constraints

react

React SpringFlingable tarot deck

Spring-physics animation primitives for React, from pmndrs

React Spring animates with real spring physics (tension, friction, mass) instead of durations, so a flung card keeps the velocity your gesture gave it. Paired with @use-gesture, useSprings drives a whole deck from one drag handler, and useTransition/looping springs handle the rest without a single keyframe.

npm i @react-spring/web @use-gesture/react
const [springs, api] = useSprings(N, (i) => ({ ...rest(i), from: fromAbove(i) }));
const bind = useDrag(({ args: [index], active, movement: [mx, my], direction: [xDir], velocity: [vx, vy] }) => {
  const trigger = vx > 0.25 || Math.abs(mx) > Math.min(window.innerWidth * 0.32, 220);
  if (!active && trigger) return fling(index, xDir || Math.sign(mx) || 1, Math.max(vx, 0.6));
  api.start((i) => {
    if (i !== index) return;
    const r = rest(i);
    return {
      x: active ? r.x + mx : r.x, y: active ? r.y + my : r.y,
      rot: active ? r.rot + mx / 9 : r.rot, scale: active ? 1.07 : 1,
      config: { tension: active ? 700 : 380, friction: active ? 40 : 24 },
    };
  });
});

ReboundOrigami spring photo grid

Facebook's Origami-era spring physics engine for JavaScript

Rebound models springs with the same tension/friction values as Facebook's Origami prototyping tool. That is where the Paper/Pop-era feel came from: anything you can map to 0→1 overshoots and settles like a physical object. One SpringSystem drives every tile here, and a second one on a SteppingSimulationLooper integrates offline to plot the exact step response for the current settings.

npm i rebound
const system = new rebound.SpringSystem();
const t = { pop: system.createSpring(tension, friction), push: system.createSpring(tension, friction) };
t.pop.addListener({ onSpringUpdate: () => applyTransform(t) });
// press: the photo pops, neighbours ripple away ring by ring
t.pop.setEndValue(1);
n.timer = setTimeout(() => n.push.setEndValue(fall), Math.max(0, k - 1) * 45);
// sliders retune every live spring
const c = rebound.SpringConfig.fromOrigamiTensionAndFriction(tension, friction);
tiles.forEach((t) => { t.pop.setSpringConfig(c); t.push.setSpringConfig(c); });
