Michael Villar's physics-based animation curves for DOM and SVG

Dynamics.js swaps cubic-bezier easing for physical models: spring with anticipation, bounce, gravity and forceWithGravity, each with a few tactile parameters. Every type is a plain function f(t), so one call both plots the curve and drives dynamics.animate. This lab recreates the original dynamicsjs.com editor: live plot with a playhead, onion-skin track and generated code.

npm i dynamics.js
dynamics.animate(ball, { translateX: dist() }, {
  type: dynamics.spring, frequency: 420, friction: 260,
  anticipationSize: 150, anticipationStrength: 220, duration: 1800,
  change: (el, t) => { playT = t; drawPlot(); },
});
// the same curve, sampled for the plot
const fn = dynamics.spring({ frequency: 420, friction: 260 });
const pts = Array.from({ length: 241 }, (_, i) => fn(i / 240));

Dice BoxWalnut-and-felt dice tray

Physics-simulated 3D game dice rolled from simple notation

Dice Box runs BabylonJS rendering and AmmoJS physics in web workers on an OffscreenCanvas, so real d4–d100 meshes tumble, collide and settle while the main thread stays free.   themeColor: '#a3202c',

});

  for (const g of groups) for (const r of g.rolls) total += r.value; // + per-die chips
};
await box.init();
box.roll(parse('3d6+1d20')); // [{ qty: 3, sides: 6, themeColor }, { qty: 1, sides: 20, themeColor }]

FractureSlow-motion shatter bento

Shatter DOM elements into slow-motion 3D shards

Fracture captures a real element to a texture, hides it, and replaces it with extruded 3D shards on a WebGL overlay. Its crack algorithm radiates and branches cracks from the impact point, so you get fine splinters near the hit and large plates farther out, which reads more like glass than Voronoi cells do. Pieces drift in slow motion with depth-of-field blur, and you can strike them again in mid-air. Here a bento grid of cards shatters wherever you tap and rebuilds itself when left idle.

npm i @abeall/fracture
stage = await createFractureStage({
  motion: { timeScale: 0.14, gravity: 620, maxShards: 1400 },
  blur: { apertureRadius: 46, maxBlurRadius: 26 },
  onFracture: (r) => results.set(r.element, r),
});
// tap a card to break it at the tap point; tap flying shards to break them again
document.addEventListener('pointerdown', async (e) => {
  const card = e.target.closest('.card');
  await stage.strike(e, { target: card && !results.has(card) ? card : null });
});
stage.restore(); // Rebuild: clear shards, un-hide every card

crt-shaderAnimated arcade title screen

Multi-pass WebGL2 CRT reconstruction for canvases, Three.js and React

Instead of overlaying scanline stripes, crt-shader rebuilds the picture in three GPU passes: horizontal signal spread, brightness-dependent beam width, then phosphor mask and optics. Bright pixels get fatter scanlines and dark ones thin out, as on a real tube. The core renderer has no dependencies and accepts any canvas, so a live procedural pixel scene can be fed through it every frame.

npm i crt-shader
import { CRTRenderer, PRESETS, resolveSettings } from 'crt-shader';

const renderer = new CRTRenderer();
function present() {
  const settings = resolveSettings(preset, overrides); // e.g. { beam, mask, glow }
  // mutable canvas source: omit sourceVersion so every frame is re-uploaded
  renderer.render(src, out, settings, { width: outSize[0], height: outSize[1] });
}

<qr-code> (bitjson)Self-assembling QR

An animate-able QR code as a single Web Component

<qr-code> renders each module, finder ring and center icon as separate SVG nodes, so animateQRCode() can stagger them by grid position: ripple out from the center, materialize at random, or fly in from your own keyframe function. This demo runs the five built-in presets plus three custom ones (Scatter, Vortex, Rain) written against the same (targets, x, y, count, entity) API.

npm i @bitjson/qr-code
defineCustomElements(window);
qr.addEventListener('codeRendered', () => qr.animateQRCode('RadialRipple'));

// custom preset: modules spiral in from the center
qr.animateQRCode((targets, x, y, count, entity) => {
  const c = count / 2, r = Math.hypot(x - c, y - c), a = Math.atan2(y - c, x - c);
  return {
    targets, from: r * 22 + ((a + Math.PI) / (2 * Math.PI)) * 260,
    duration: 600, easing: 'cubic-bezier(.3,0,.2,1)',
    web: { opacity: [0, 1], rotate: [180, 0], scale: [0, 1] },
  };
});

perfect-cursorsRaw vs spline multiplayer cursors

Spline interpolation for throttled multiplayer cursor updates

Steve Ruiz's tiny library behind tldraw's live cursors: feed it the positions your socket delivers at 4-15 Hz and it animates a smooth spline through them at display rate. The left board teleports to each packet; the right board renders the same packets through PerfectCursor, with its interpolated trail drawn behind each collaborator.

npm i perfect-cursors
import { PerfectCursor } from 'perfect-cursors';

cur.pc = new PerfectCursor((pt) => {
  cur.smooth = [pt[0] / 1000, pt[1] / 1000];   // called every frame
});

// whenever a (throttled, jittery) network packet arrives:
c.nextSend = now + (1000 / HZ) * (0.75 + Math.random() * 0.5);
c.raw = c.p.slice();                            // what you'd draw without it
c.pc.addPoint([c.p[0] * 1000, c.p[1] * 1000]);

AtramentSumi-e ink sketchbook

Tiny canvas library for smooth, ink-like drawing and handwriting

Atrament smooths every stroke and modulates its width by drawing speed or stylus pressure, so lines taper like a real pen instead of plotting at a fixed width. Here its programmatic beginStroke/draw/endStroke API brushes an ensō and a plum branch, its worker-based flood fill colours the blossoms and wash hills, and erase mode carves the seal. Then the brush is yours.

npm i atrament
const atr = new Atrament(inkCv, { width: Math.round(w * DPR), height: Math.round(h * DPR), color: INK.sumi, fill });

// auto-draw: one brush stroke through the programmatic API
atr.mode = op.mode; atr.color = op.color; atr.weight = op.weight;
atr.beginStroke(p[0], p[1]);
auto.prev = atr.draw(x, y, auto.prev.x, auto.prev.y, pr); // per point, pr = brush pressure
atr.endStroke(auto.prev.x, auto.prev.y);

// then flood-fill the blossom outlines (fill worker from 'atrament/fill')
atr.mode = MODE_FILL; atr.color = op.color;
for (const [x, y] of op.pts) fillAt(x, y);

drauuPresenter slide annotations

Headless SVG drawing and annotation engine, the pen behind Slidev

drauu turns any <svg> into a drawing surface: a pressure-aware perfect-freehand stylus, lines with arrowheads, dashed rectangles, ellipses, a line eraser and undo/redo, all saved as plain SVG elements you can style or dump(). Here synthetic pen events go through drauu's own pointer listeners, so a virtual presenter marks up a QBR slide and then hands you the pen.

npm i drauu
const drauu = createDrauu({ el: svg, brush: { mode: 'stylus', color: COLORS.yellow, size: 6 } });

// the presenter: switch tool, then drive drauu with real PointerEvents
drauu.mode = g.mode; // 'stylus' | 'line' | 'rectangle' | 'ellipse' | 'eraseLine'
Object.assign(drauu.brush, { arrowEnd: false, dasharray: undefined, cornerRadius: 0 }, g.brush);
fire('pointerdown', x, y, p);
fire('pointermove', x, y, p); // once per sampled point, at rAF pace
fire('pointerup', x, y, p);

$('#undo').addEventListener('click', () => { stopAuto(); drauu.undo(); });

/>

p5.jsNoise flow field

Processing's creative-coding sketchbook, reborn for the browser

p5.js keeps Processing's setup()/draw() mental model: immediate-mode drawing, built-in Perlin noise and an event loop you never have to wire up. Thousands of particles riding a noise field with additive trails take about sixty lines in instance mode, so it slots into any bundle without globals.

npm i p5
new p5((p) => {
  p.draw = () => {
    p.fill(...pal.bg, 14); p.rect(0, 0, p.width, p.height);
    for (const q of parts) {
      const a = p.noise(q.x * sc, q.y * sc, zoff) * p.TWO_PI * 2.5;
      q.x += Math.cos(a) * 1.6; q.y += Math.sin(a) * 1.6;
      p.stroke(q.c); p.line(q.px, q.py, q.x, q.y);
    }
  };
  p.mousePressed = () => reseed();
}, document.getElementById('stage'));

vanilla

Elementary AudioLive-coded phosphor scope

Declarative, functional audio DSP: describe the graph, it diffs it

Elementary treats sound like React treats UI: you return a tree of el.* nodes and the wasm engine reconciles it against what is already playing, so edits re-render without clicks or restarts. Here the same patch drives a realtime AudioWorklet and an offline renderer that paints the L/R XY scope before you ever press play.

npm i @elemaudio/core @elemaudio/web-renderer @elemaudio/offline-renderer
const clock = el.train(7);
const hz = el.seq({ seq: notes, loop: true }, clock, 0);
const env = el.adsr(0.004, 0.14, 0.15, 0.1, clock);
const cut = el.add(180, el.mul(2600, env));
const l = el.lowpass(cut, 7, el.blepsaw(hz));

// on every edit: re-evaluate, then reconcile both engines
const [l, r] = new Function('el', codeEl.value)(el);
await offline.render(l, r);           // drives the scope
if (live) await live.render(l, r);    // WebRenderer → AudioWorklet

vanilla

Tone.jsFM step sequencer

A Web Audio framework with synths, effects and a musical transport

Tone.js wraps raw Web Audio in musician vocabulary: '16n' note values, a sample-accurate Transport, PolySynths, reverbs and feedback delays you chain like pedals. Tone.getDraw() syncs DOM updates to scheduled audio time, which is why the playhead never drifts from the beat.

npm i tone
synth = new Tone.PolySynth(Tone.FMSynth, { harmonicity: 2, modulationIndex: 6 }).connect(delay);
kik = new Tone.MembraneSynth({ pitchDecay: 0.04, octaves: 6 }).connect(master);

transport.scheduleRepeat((time) => {
  const s = step % 16;
  for (let r = 0; r < ROWS.length; r++) if (state[r][s]) trigger(r, time);
  Tone.getDraw().schedule(() => setHead(s), time);
  step++;
}, '16n');

PtsVoronoi stained glass

A library for visualizing and expressing ideas through points

  const de = Create.delaunay(new Group(...sites.map((s) => s.p), ptr.clone()));
  const tris = de.delaunay(true);
  de.voronoi(space.innerBound).forEach((cell, i) => {
    const c = Polygon.centroid(cell);
    const poly = cell.map((p) => c.$add(p.$subtract(c).multiply(inset)));
    form.fillOnly(hexA(sites[i].c, 0.07 + k * 0.75)).polygon(poly);
  });
}});
space.bindMouse().bindTouch().play();

html5bytebeatBytebeat formula lab

One-line math expressions of t rendered as 8 kHz audio

Gregg Tavares' bytebeat engine compiles a JavaScript expression like t*(t>>5|t>>8) and runs it per sample inside an AudioWorklet, in bytebeat, floatbeat or postfix modes. The demo runs the library's own compiler and ByteBeatProcessor on the main thread too, so the scrolling t-plot (256 samples per column), oscilloscope and spectrum draw the formula before any sound plays.

node.setDesiredSampleRate(rate);
await node.setExpressions([expr], true);
node.connect(analyser);
// same compiler on the main thread drives the visuals
local.setExpressions([compiled.expression]);
const s = local.getSampleForTime(tDone, lctx, lstack);

const [instruments, patterns, sequence, bpm] = song;
// one channel per call, so each voice can be scoped and muted
const solo = patterns.map((p) => [p[c] && p[c].length ? p[c] : [0, 0, ...new Array(p[0].length - 2).fill(0)]]);
const [l, r] = zzfxM(instruments, solo, sequence, bpm);
const L = Float32Array.from(l), R = Float32Array.from(r);
self.postMessage({ id, c, channels, L, R, rate: zzfxR }, [L.buffer, R.buffer]);

PitchyAnalog needle chromatic tuner

Tiny McLeod Pitch Method pitch detector for any audio buffer

Pitchy runs the McLeod Pitch Method (FFT autocorrelation + normalized square difference) on a plain Float32Array and returns [pitch, clarity] — no AudioWorklet or framework required. else synthWindow(input);
const [pitch, clarity] = detector.findPitch(input, sr);
det.ok = clarity > 0.85 && pitch > 55 && pitch < 1800;
const m = hzToMidi(pitch); // -> note name, cents, needle

Pink TromboneTalking vocal tract

Headless, polyphonic port of Neil Thapen's vocal tract speech synthesizer

A physical model of the throat, mouth and nose: a 44-segment waveguide driven by an LF glottal pulse, so moving the tongue or closing the lips changes the sound. This package strips Thapen's UI and exposes normalized vowel, constriction, pitch and nasality controls, and lets you run several voices at once. The demo redraws his pink tract from the library's live diameters. It babbles words on its own until you take over, and choir mode stacks three trombones.

t.vowel.frontness = 1;            // tongue forward…
t.vowel.openness = 0.03;          // …and high: [i]
const lips = t.constrictions.add(0.93, 1); // close lips: [m]/[b]
t.nasality = 1;                   // lower the velum
t.pitch = 52;                     // MIDI note
t.isVoiced = true;
// draw the live tract shape
for (let i = 1; i < t.tract.n; i++) lineTo(...P(i, t.tract.diameter[i]));

binjgbDMG with a rewind tape

Tiny, accurate Game Boy emulator compiled to WebAssembly

binjgb is Ben Smith's cycle-accurate Game Boy emulator: an 88 KB wasm file with a plain C API for frames, audio, save states and a delta-compressed rewind buffer. Here it runs in a CSS-drawn DMG. A bot plays by reading the game's RAM, and when it dies it rewinds the tape and tries again. Game: Tobu Tobu Girl by Tangram Games (code MIT, assets CC BY 4.0).

curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/binji/binjgb/16621111ed0ee73bcc45c912a823bcebedcffc0f/docs/binjgb.{js,wasm}
const mod = await window.Binjgb({ wasmBinary: wasm });
const e = mod._emulator_new_simple(romPtr, size, 44100, 4096, 0);
const rw = mod._rewind_new_simple(e, 45, 8 * 1024 * 1024);
// each frame: run, then append to the rewind tape
const ev = mod._emulator_run_until_f64(e, ticks);
if (ev & EVENT_NEW_FRAME) mod._rewind_append(rw, e);
// scrub: jump to any tick in the buffered past
const st = mod._rewind_begin(e, rw, joypad);
mod._rewind_to_ticks_wrapper(st, targetTicks);

Phaser 4 rebuilds the renderer around filters: any camera or game object gets internal/external filter lists (Glow, Blur, Barrel, Pixelate, Vignette, ColorMatrix, Bokeh, Displacement...) plus composite Actions like AddEffectBloom. This attract-mode brick-breaker stacks bloom, vignette and a barrel pulse on the camera, glows the bricks, ball and paddle, and fires pixelate and hue-sweep bursts on combos and wave clears. this.brickLayer.enableFilters();
this.fx.brickGlow = this.brickLayer.filters.external.addGlow(0xff2e88, 3.2, 0, 1, false, 8, 8);

// full-screen camera stack: bloom → vignette → barrel pulse → pixelate burst → colour matrix
const cam = this.cameras.main;
this.fx.bloom = Phaser.Actions.AddEffectBloom(cam, { threshold: 0.42, blurRadius: 3, blurSteps: 4, blendAmount: 0.85 })[0];
this.fx.vignette = cam.filters.external.addVignette(0.5, 0.5, 0.76, 0.1);
this.fx.barrel = cam.filters.external.addBarrel(1);
this.fx.pixelate = cam.filters.external.addPixelate(1);

ExcaliburCRT pixel-art platformer

TypeScript-first 2D game engine for the web

Excalibur's pixelArt mode keeps sprites crisp while they move at sub-pixel positions and the camera eases, so you don't have to snap to integer coordinates. Its PostProcessor API takes your own GLSL fragment shader and runs it over the finished frame. Here that shader adds a curved tube, scanlines, chromatic aberration and a vignette to an endless attract-mode run. The scene also uses arcade physics, one-way platforms, ParallaxComponent layers, sprite-sheet animations and particle bursts. All art is generated at runtime.

npm i excalibur
class CrtPostProcessor {
  initialize(gctx) { this.screen = new ex.ScreenShader(gctx, CRT_FRAG); }
  getShader() { return this.screen.getShader(); }
  getLayout() { return this.screen.getLayout(); }
  onUpdate(elapsed) {
    this.on += (this.target - this.on) * Math.min(1, elapsed / 90);
    this.getShader().trySetUniformFloat('u_on', this.on);
    this.getShader().trySetUniformFloatVector('u_game', this.game);
  }
}
engine.graphicsContext.addPostProcessor(new CrtPostProcessor());

Uxn5Varvara desktop, three ROMs

Hundred Rabbits' JS/wasm emulator for the Uxn/Varvara computer

Uxn is a 32-opcode stack machine and Varvara is the tiny computer built around it: a 4-colour palette that each ROM sets, 2-bit sprites on two layers, and devices for the screen, mouse and controller. Uxn5 runs those ROMs in the browser and fits in a few kB of plain script plus a wasm core. This demo boots an original Uxntal toy, 100r's Catclock and the card game Donsol, all built with the official drifloon assembler.

git clone https://git.sr.ht/~rabbits/uxn5
const emu = new window.Emu(true);
emu.init();
// ...boot(r): swap programs on the running machine
const rom = await getRom(r);
s.vector = 0; // stop the previous ROM's frame vector before swapping programs
s.resize(f.sw, f.sh, 1);
emu.load(rom); // uxn5 API: resets the core, copies the ROM to 0x100 and evaluates the reset vector
s.set_zoom(z);
// touch: feed the finger position to the mouse device before its pointerdown
frame.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => { emu.mouse.on_move(e); }, true);

v86bootOS on a beige PC

x86 PC emulator with an x86-to-WebAssembly JIT

v86 emulates a whole PC (CPU, VGA, floppy controller, PIT, keyboard) and JIT-compiles guest x86 code to WebAssembly, so real BIOSes and operating systems boot in a tab. Here SeaBIOS boots nanochess's 512-byte bootOS from a floppy image assembled in JS at runtime. An autopilot reads the emulated VGA text buffer to play Bricks, then the demo moves on to a raycaster, bootBASIC and a pi calculator.

npm i v86
const fda = await buildFloppy();          // 1.44 MB bootOS disk assembled in JS
emulator = new V86({
  wasm_path: wasmUrl,
  screen: { container: $('#screen'), use_graphical_text: true },
  bios: { url: biosUrl },
  vga_bios: { url: vgaBiosUrl },
  fda: { buffer: fda },
  autostart: true,
  disable_mouse: true,
  disable_speaker: true,   // PC speaker voiced via pcspeaker-* bus events instead
});
const rows = emulator.screen_adapter.get_text_screen();

PuzzleScriptMirror-twin push puzzle

A whole puzzle game as one short text file of rules

PuzzleScript games are plain text: 5x5 pixel sprites, sfxr sound seeds, collision layers and pattern-rewrite rules like [ > Player | Crate ] -> [ > Player | > Crate ]. This original 4-level game runs on the unmodified engine; the source sits beside it and each rule line lights up as the engine applies it.

git clone https://github.com/increpare/PuzzleScript (or File > Export standalone HTML on puzzlescript.net)
(the twin mirrors you left/right, follows you up/down)
[ left  Player ] [ Twin ] -> [ left  Player ] [ right Twin ]
[ right Player ] [ Twin ] -> [ right Player ] [ left  Twin ]

(pits stop walkers but swallow crates)
[ > Walker | Pit ] -> [ Walker | Pit ]
[ > Walker | Crate ] -> [ > Walker | > Crate ]

late [ Crate Pit ] -> [ Bridge ]
late [ Crate Target ] -> [ Crate Target Glow ]

LittleJSNeon particle brick-breaker

Tiny, fast WebGL 2D game engine with particles, sound and shaders

LittleJS draws batched WebGL sprites, runs a ParticleEmitter system, plays ZzFX sound and adds a Shadertoy-style post-process pass, and the whole engine is small enough for a game jam. Here every hit sets off additive particle bursts and camera shake, and the bloom, chromatic split and scanlines come from the engine's own post-process effect functions. Nothing in the demo is loaded from an image file.

npm i littlejsengine
new PostProcessPlugin(postProcessEffects(
  postProcessChromatic(.0011),
  postProcessGlow(.3, 1.25, 7),
  postProcessScanlines(.16, 3 * px),
  postProcessVignette(.85, 2.6),
  'c.rgb = pow(c.rgb, vec3(.95)) * vec3(1.02, .98, 1.06);'));
const e = new ParticleEmitter(
  pos, opts.angle ?? 0, opts.emitSize ?? .4, .08, count / .08, opts.cone ?? PI, undefined,
  color, color.lerp(WHITE_C, .6), color.scale(1, 0), rgb(.3, .1, .9, 0),
  opts.life ?? .7, size, opts.sizeEnd ?? .02, speed, .15, .9, .9, opts.gravity ?? 1, PI, .4, .6,
  false, true, true, 1e5);
e.trailScale = opts.trail ?? 2.2;

About this page

Each demo is a small page built against the library's own npm package or registry, bundled with Vite and served from this domain: no CDNs, no hotlinked assets. Demos load as you scroll and unload when you leave, so only a handful run at once. Open any of them full-window with ↗.
